title: Siding With Putin Is a Huge Mistake
excerpt: President Trump’s inexplicable decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, announced late Friday, essentially gives a pass to the forces of evil in the Kremlin
body: President Trump’s inexplicable decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, announced late Friday, essentially gives a pass to the forces of evil in the Kremlin

The move effectively nullifies legislation that was named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, passed by huge bipartisan majorities in both the House and Senate, and signed by the president
This decision is the latest in a long series that this administration has taken to appease or accommodate the Russians in misguided attempts to get them to negotiate
Russian President Vladimir Putin pockets these naive offerings and still refuses to talk

Surveys show that most Americans stand with Ukraine as it defends itself against Russia, view Putin as a dangerous threat who shouldn’t be trusted, and want to see the United States offer more assistance to Ukraine
Few wars in recent history have been so black-and-white: Russia is the guilty party that invaded Ukraine for no good reason
Ukraine is, for its part, defending its freedom, sovereignty, and territorial integrity
And yet there is much misinformation and disinformation circulating that blurs the picture
To address the problem of phony narratives, it is useful to contrast Russia and Putin with Ukraine and its president, Volodymyr Zelensky

Putin came to power in August 1999, when his predecessor, Boris Yeltsin, designated him prime minister and his preferred successor; Yeltsin resigned from office at the end of that year and named Putin acting president, three months before the next presidential election
Putin had used his time as prime minister to deploy brutal force against the Chechens in 1999
Zelensky became the leader of Ukraine in 2019, when he won by a landslide in a free and fair election certified by domestic and international observers
Putin hasn’t won a legitimate election throughout his two-plus decades in power
Putin is a murderous dictator who kills his own citizens as well as those of his neighbors

Zelensky is a democratically elected leader whose term has been extended because Ukraine cannot credibly conduct elections under martial law, which was declared after Russia invaded on a full scale in 2022
Under Putin, Russian forces deliberately target civilian areas, including hospitals, apartment buildings, and schools
They also seek to destroy energy facilities and water supplies to freeze out Ukrainians and force them into submission
Zelensky and Ukrainian forces focus on Russian energy facilities that provide Putin with funding for his war campaign, but generally seek to minimize civilian casualties
Putin first started the war against Ukraine in 2014, when he illegally annexed Crimea and then moved into Ukraine’s Donbas region
Zelensky wasn’t even in politics that year, so he can’t be blamed for starting the war
Putin refuses to end the war, enter serious negotiations, or even entertain a cease-fire

Zelensky and Ukraine have shown tremendous willingness to negotiate, freeze the fighting at its current stage, and sort out the status of Russian-occupied land through diplomacy, without conferring recognition of Russian control
Putin has ignored Trump’s repeated efforts to end the war, including the recent energy-cease-fire announcement , by continuing to strike Ukrainian energy targets
Zelensky had suspended retaliatory strikes against Russian refineries for three days but lifted that pause after Russia kept bombing Ukraine
Putin sought to topple the Zelensky government through his full-scale invasion, in 2022, to take over massive amounts of Ukrainian territory and to subjugate the country under Russian rule
Zelensky and the people of Ukraine simply have sought to live in peace and exercise their right to determine their independent future
Putin wishes to challenge and undermine democratic nations and the institutions that bring them together, such as NATO and the European Union
Ukraine seeks to join these institutions and assume its rightful place as a full member of the Euro-Atlantic community
Putin supports Iran against the United States, providing both intelligence aimed to target and kill Americans as well as weapons systems to help that cause
Zelensky and Ukraine offered the United States and its allies in the Middle East anti-drone capabilities and insights on how to fight the Iranian Shahed drones, which have been used against Ukraine
Putin relies on North Koreans and others who have been trafficked into Russia’s side of the war
Casualties are merely a statistic for him and for North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong Un
Zelensky has never asked the West to send its troops to fight on Ukraine’s side, but he does seek Western assistance to defend against the much larger Russian military
Putin depends on China’s purchases of Russian energy and provision of dual-use technology to back his war
Ukraine looks to the West for its support
Putin and Russia are key parts of CRINK , the grouping of the authoritarian regimes in China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea that seek to weaken and threaten the West
Ukraine is the bulwark against a major part of this dangerous alignment
Putin and Russian forces have launched provocations against Europe and the United States, almost daring war with the West

These have included major violations of NATO airspace; drone attacks and interference with European airports and flights; assassinations and attempted killings on Western soil; cyberattacks; and election interference
Ukraine stands between Russia and Europe, fighting for its freedom as well as the safety and security of the continent

title: America Is Now an Ally of Russia
excerpt: In the past week, the president of the United States has conclusively turned America into an ally of the Russian Federation
body: In the past week, the president of the United States has conclusively turned America into an ally of the Russian Federation
Donald Trump has now abandoned pretense and is openly aiding the Kremlin in its war against a friend and partner of the U.S
The American commander in chief has abandoned the Western order, the most successful—and powerful—security arrangement in human history
To judge from the available evidence, he has not done so out of a cold calculation of the national interest

Instead, he has based his decisions on his own interests; his open admiration for Russia’s dictator; his resentment of Ukraine’s democratically elected president; and quite possibly other factors that so far have remained obscured from the American public
In September, Trump signed a sanctions bill that Congress had passed, named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a pro-Ukraine hawk
The legislation sanctioned Russia as well as other countries that are supporting Russia’s invasion and brutalization of Ukraine

The bill was approved with bipartisan support, but some Republicans and most House Democrats voted against the law, arguing that it contained a trap door, a provision that would allow Trump to suspend the prescribed sanctions at will
Trump pulled the lever on that trap door just two days before the law was supposed to go into effect

In an executive order signed on Friday, Trump said that “such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States”—he declined to explain exactly how the waiver was in America’s interests—and that the law would remain unexecuted until such time as his administration decides otherwise
This waiver came a short while after Trump lifted restrictions on Russia’s sales of diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets

Trump’s recent actions in support of Russia are so obvious that they have generated a rare moment of bipartisan disgust: Both Democrats and Republicans now seem to share a horror at the betrayal of Ukraine, and at the president’s reckless abdication of America’s role as leader of the free world
The president’s aides are scrambling to explain why this capitulation to Russia isn’t exactly what it looks like
Secretary of State Marco Rubio , when pressed by a reporter, said that the administration would “assess” the impact of the Graham Act after a 60-day period
This was nonsense: The executive order includes no such timeline, and no one seriously believes that the administration is running numbers to decide whether sanctions are a good idea
Rubio was joined in his excuse making by a handful of desperate Republicans who tried to cast Trump’s decision as some sort of tough-love patriotism

When asked on Sunday whether he agreed with Trump on lifting sanctions, Senator James Lankford of Oklahoma said, “He is choosing the American people first, is what he’s doing.” But few even on the American right seem willing to buy it
Trump loyalist Senator Ted Cruz called Trump’s move “a mistake,” and Senator Darline Graham, who now holds her brother’s seat, broke with Trump as well
Some conservative commentators, including Andy McCarthy, a former federal prosecutor who writes for National Review , expressed considerably more rage

McCarthy wrote on Saturday that Putin is on a “quest to reconstitute America’s Soviet enemy,” and that “President Donald Trump is giving him aid and comfort.” As a lawyer, McCarthy surely did not choose those words at random
Aid and comfort are part of the criteria in Article III of the Constitution of the United States that define treason
McCarthy called for “immediate hearings about this week’s shocking escalation of the Trump-Putin alliance.” Trump’s decision has nothing to do with American national security
His de facto alliance with Russia is a sordid arrangement rooted in his own fears and hatreds

First, Trump knows that Republicans are almost certainly facing a beating in the midterm elections, in part over the price of gas—a spike caused by the kind of war in Iran that he promised during his 2024 campaign to never start

He is desperate to do anything he can to lower the price of gas, and because he does not seem to understand how the international economy works, he may well believe that some janky diesel deal with Russia will alleviate high fuel prices in the United States. (It will not, although it will certainly help some Russian companies.) As Malcolm Rifkind, a former defense minister of the United Kingdom, put it this weekend: “Donald Trump has shown himself as a person to be repulsive; as a President of the United States to be a disgrace to his own people as well as to his international responsibilities

We all know his actual reasons for this are a grubby attempt to win a few more votes in the midterms by trying to get oil prices down.” The result, Rifkind rightly added, is that Trump will now be “directly responsible” for the deaths of Ukrainians who will die while Putin uses the Russian alliance with America to continue the fighting
But even if the American economy were in better shape, Trump’s history with Putin suggests that he was never going to allow the sanctions in the Graham Act to be enforced
Trump’s suspension of the law is a signal to Ukraine, to Russia, to Europe, and to America’s NATO allies that the Trump White House and Putin’s Kremlin are now on the same side
Trump’s man-crush on the Russian dictator has been well documented and need not be recounted in all its unctuous detail

His attachment is so obvious that for years it has sparked various complicated theories about its origins, but Occam’s razor suggests a more direct explanation: Trump is a weak man who is intimidated by stronger and smarter men

His humiliating relationship with Putin is different only in degree from the way he interacts with other authoritarian leaders, including China’s Xi Jinping and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un (a dangerous totalitarian with whom Trump claimed to have fallen in love)
As if to prove the point, this afternoon Trump posted a whiny screed on his Truth Social site in which he pleaded with the public to understand how overmatched he is against Putin

Trump tried to explain that he is accommodating the Russian leader because he doesn’t “want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” In a deeply pathetic admission, he warned that angering Putin could have consequences in Iran: “Perhaps more importantly, Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way.” He then said that Zelensky has gotten so much money from the Biden administration and from Europe that “he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.” Consider what the American president just told the entire world: Please don’t interfere in my relationship with a murderous dictator, or he might help the country that America’s men and women in uniform are fighting at this very moment

The leader of the most powerful nation on the planet—yes, that’s still the United States right now—is trying to get everyone else, including the American Congress, to avoid antagonizing Putin, instead of warning Putin not to even think about aiding Iran
Nothing better illustrates just how weak a supplicant Trump has become in his relationship with the Kremlin boss
Trump engages in this kind of personalized diplomacy in part because he believes himself to be—against all evidence—a master dealmaker
But the greater irony, considering how much he rails against globalism, is that he also behaves this way because he is in fact a globalist himself
He does not view the world as a collection of sovereign nations; he sees it instead as territories run by mob bosses
The weaker ones, especially America’s allies, can be abused and threatened at will
The stronger godfathers, including America’s dedicated enemies, are peers and thus treated with respect

title: How the Rabbit Revolution Went Too Far
excerpt: T his is the moment I knew that the whole vibrator thing had gone too far: It was about a year ago, and I’d ordered a replacement rabbit, the model I’d fallen f
body: T his is the moment I knew that the whole vibrator thing had gone too far: It was about a year ago, and I’d ordered a replacement rabbit, the model I’d fallen for around 2007, amid the vibrator renaissance brought about by Sex and the City

An early episode of that zeitgeist show features the prudish Charlotte, having reluctantly bought a “Rabbit Pearl” on the advice of her friend Miranda, becoming so addicted to her new toy that she stops leaving her apartment, thus turning the rabbit into a cultural icon for female pleasure

More than a quarter century had passed since that innocent moment, and the rabbit—once a battery-operated device with a clunky rotating shaft and dainty bunny ears that shivered with astonishing proficiency—had turned sleek and space-age
The rabbits I ordered had USB chargers and a variety of speeds
They had safety locks and silencers, like guns

I didn’t want all these added features—22 speeds was about 20 too many—but I could never remember the name of the most recent one I’d ordered, so I had to Google best rabbit vibrators , a quest that once upon a time had taken me to niche women’s websites but now took me to The New York Times ’ Wirecutter
It’s not that the newer rabbit models don’t work; it’s that they do too much
I mean, I wouldn’t buy a spatula that also dusted the floor
My latest model was so fancy and complicated that it took me a while to figure out how to switch it on, but the real problem was that, once it was on, I could not figure out how to turn the thing off

The day I received it, I was about to record a podcast, a detail that sounds irrelevant until you realize what I was up against: I could not have a vibrator droning on in the background of an hour-long audio conversation
I spent minutes that felt like hours desperately pushing three buttons in alternating sequences only to be thwarted—the rabbit would not turn off
It thumped, it jittered, it whirred round and round
I determined that the only way to shut the damn thing up would be to run down its battery
Racing to beat the clock before the podcast began, I bolted to my front door to place the infernal device outside, where its insistent whirring wouldn’t be picked up by the mic
Just before I got there, I somehow hit the right sequence, and the vibrator finally shut down
What a sad modern portrait: a single woman, living alone, with a rabbit vibrator jackhammering haplessly against her door

Around that time, I happened to be listening to Dax Shepard’s Armchair Expert podcast when I heard a sex therapist say, “Turn down the speed on your vibrators.” Shepard—a modern man in the sex-positive mold—sounded confused; he seemed to be under the impression that vibrators were good for women
Weren’t we all? I ’d been thinking about turning down the speed on my vibrator for a long time, but I’d considered my affliction personal, not society-wide
Now it was dawning on me that the problem wasn’t simply mine
Women are being sold egg-shaped suction devices in the pages of New York magazine, and BookTok influencers pair with sex-toy companies for promotional collabs

Yes, there is a bookmark that doubles as a vibrator. (“Building a world where women choose their pleasure + their power,” reads the Instagram bio for Her Little Bookmark.) Does this consumer game of one-upmanship amid the mainstreaming of vibrators even matter? There are too many varieties of women’s razors, too, and I don’t care
But what worries me is how this points in the direction in which so much of modern life has been barreling: self-pleasure, self-love, self-care, self, self, self
This is where my mind goes when I read or hear a certain type of brittle “Don’t need a man, I have a vibrator” argument, a flex that’s been prevalent on social media for at least a decade
I’d love to see a chart of the well-documented sex recession laid across a chart of vibrator sales

A vibrator may get you off better than a man (or a woman, for that matter), but will it clean the gutters? Hold you in the dark? Kill the rat skittering around the attic? I write these words, and then I think: But wait, what if one day it can? I arrived late to vibrators, or perhaps I should say masturbation, in the relatively vibrator-shy ’90s
I was a few years out of college, sharing pitchers of beer with my buddy Aaron, and we were about halfway through the second pitcher when I shared a very personal detail: I’d never had an orgasm

Not ever? Aaron was fascinated but not judgmental; in fact, another female friend had recently confessed something similar, and he’d researched the problem late one night (he was in law school, and miserable) and discovered that her predicament was both common and easy to solve. “You need the Cadillac of vibrators,” he said, referring to the Hitachi Magic Wand, a personal massager that resembled a large white microphone
The Hitachi, he’d learned, launched women into such paroxysms of pleasure that it had acquired cult status
And he’d heard that you could buy it at Walmart
Walmart had famously eighty-sixed popular albums by Marilyn Manson and (of all people) Sheryl Crow, but Aaron explained that this was part of the ruse
All of those “personal massagers” I’d seen in Sharper Image catalogs? Those were vibrators
Why else were they waterproof? I had to admit that he had a point. [ From the September 2026 issue: The great romance slump ] We drove to Walmart but it didn’t have the Cadillac of vibrators
Unwilling to end our adventure, Aaron picked up an alternate model he declared the “Ford Taurus of vibrators.” The picture on the front resembled a plug-in hand mixer

That night, alone in my garage apartment, I unwrapped the box, drank some red wine to set the mood, and plugged the Ford Taurus of vibrators into an outlet, only to discover that the cord didn’t reach the bed
Was there an extension cord around? Never mind
I lay down nervously on a small braided rug, staring at the slowly rotating blades of the ceiling fan, and turned on the power, only to discover that hell no
It felt like industrial turbines were juddering against my most sensitive spot
Back in high school, my mother had given me a Brookstone mini-massager she’d bought at the mall, a stocking stuffer for a teen daughter with D cups and upper-back pain
I’d been lugging it from apartment to apartment like a kitchen utensil I never used
It was demure and beige, the size of a small flashlight, and it was waterproof

title: Are We Too Political?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube One of the paradoxes of our moment is that the excesses of Donald Trump’s presidency seem to demand our obses
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube One of the paradoxes of our moment is that the excesses of Donald Trump’s presidency seem to demand our obsessive attention, while Trump himself obviously thrives on that attention—and all of the social division that comes with it

What if the clearest way out of our political crisis is taking politics less seriously? In this episode of The Permanent Questions , David Brooks speaks with his old friend (and new boss), Atlantic editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg, about the pleasures and pitfalls of a life spent covering politicians, the limits of partisanship, and the need to see life from the redwood’s perspective
The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Our topic today is politics
What role should politics play in your life? How much of your spiritual, emotional, and mental energy should you devote to politics? Now, I am something of a political junkie

I grew up as a political correspondent covering people, and I can say there’s nothing more fun in journalism than going to a rally in Iowa or New Hampshire or anywhere people are campaigning, talking with the folks, watching them scream, watching the passion
It’s just Americana in all its glory, both good and bad
They’re good people in rotten circumstances
And yet I also feel that we’ve over-politicized our society
What car you drive is determined by red or blue
The TV shows you watch are determined by red or blue
Who you marry and befriend, how you think about the WNBA
When you make politics your religion, you think you have a sense of belonging, but you really don’t
You’re not sitting with your community members; you’re just hating the same people
You have the illusion of righteous action
You’re doing something good for the country
But you’re not feeding the poor or sitting with the widow; you’re just hating people on social media
It gives you the illusion of all the things that you get in a real community or a real faith or a real philosophy, but you just end up in a cultural war
I’m trying to figure out: How do I care about politics without over-caring? My guest today is Jeffrey Goldberg
You probably know him as the editor in chief of The Atlantic magazine
As you watch or listen to this conversation, you will notice that Jeff and I know each other
You’ll see that we have, as all old friends do, a certain way of talking to each other
We have a certain banter, which involves a lot of interruption
What you are about to witness is us at our most slow paced, our most earnest, our most serious
Jeff and I will be talking about what role politics should play in our lives
But in order to get there, I thought we’d compare notes about our careers, the politicians we’ve covered, what we’ve thought about them, what’s been important, what’s been unimportant
Jeffrey Goldberg, welcome to The Permanent Questions
Brooks: This must be— Goldberg: I’m very wary
You do edit a magazine, you’ve won some prizes, but this really is pretty much the pinnacle of your career
Goldberg: You know, I applied to Yale, and I got rejected
They were just like, “What, are you joking?” So I consider this getting into Yale
Aren’t you a professor at Yale? Brooks: I’m a faculty member at Yale
Goldberg: What does that mean? What’s the difference between a professor and a faculty member? Brooks: Professors know what they’re talking about
Brooks: We’re going to talk politics, if we can get on track here, which is highly unlikely
Brooks: We’ve spent our lives covering this stuff
So I’m gonna ask you, I want to get your political origin story
Goldberg: My political origin story? Brooks: When did you first have a brush with politics? Goldberg: My first brush with politics was when, as a 2-year-old, I urinated on Al Shanker’s lap
Do you remember Al Shanker? Brooks: Of course
He was head of the American Federation of Teachers
Goldberg: He led the 1968 teachers’ strike
My father was one of the leaders of the teachers’ strike

title: The Evolution of the Human Brain Set It Up for Failure
excerpt: Apes don’t develop Alzheimer’s—at least, not like we do
body: Apes don’t develop Alzheimer’s—at least, not like we do
Although we share a hefty amount of our DNA with our closest primate relatives, humans are uniquely at risk of developing the disease that can erode our sense of who we are
When I make the diagnosis in my neurology clinic, I tell patients and family members that in most cases, doctors can’t point to a single, definitive cause of the illness
Age, genetics, health, lifestyle factors, and environmental triggers all play a role
But a growing body of research offers another dimension: We can lose our sense of self precisely because our species evolved to have one
In recent years, scientists have been comparing the brains of humans with those of other, closely related species, and teasing out how the genetics, structure, and molecular mechanisms differ
What they’re finding is that the same characteristics that support our unparalleled cognitive abilities make us susceptible to Alzheimer’s disease
Certainly, the biological hallmarks of Alzheimer’s look different inside the human brain than in the brains of other species

Melissa Edler, a comparative neurobiologist at Kent State University, and her team have identified distinct patterns in how humans and chimpanzees accumulate amyloid plaques and tau tangles, the toxic proteins that build up in brains with Alzheimer’s
She believes that looking at multiple species is going to be crucial to understanding how this disease develops

If nonhuman primates aren’t developing Alzheimer’s, “why aren’t they?” she asked, when we spoke about her work. “What’s different about their brains?” One answer dates back to the early 2000s, when the Swedish geneticist Svante Pääbo (who went on to win the Nobel Prize for sequencing the Neanderthal genome) wondered what might account for the profound behavioral differences between humans and other apes—after all, we build civilizations while nonhuman primates cannot, without assistance, start a fire
Pääbo and his team of international researchers collected brain, blood, and liver tissue from humans, chimpanzees, orangutans, and macaques

But instead of comparing the genes themselves, they measured the genes’ activity—effectively, how hard each gene was working to make messenger RNA, which carries instructions from DNA on how to make proteins
Gene activity in the liver and blood, they found, was roughly equivalent across the species they tested
But activity in the human brain had ramped up
Pääbo hadn’t set out to study Alzheimer’s specifically, but his findings hinted at a link between evolution and brain disease that others have pursued more directly

In a study published in 2020, for instance, Thomas Arendt, a neuroscientist at Leipzig University, and his team looked at autopsied brain samples from people with and without Alzheimer’s disease and found nearly 300 genes whose level of activity was different in the Alzheimer’s brains

When they looked at those particular genes more closely, they found that their genetic sequences had undergone a lot of change in a short amount of time—an indication that those genes played an important role in the human brain’s rapid and distinctive evolution. “In other words,” Arendt told me recently, “Alzheimer’s disease is based on changes in the genome that are typically human.” Other researchers, too, have gathered evidence that supports the idea that evolution and Alzheimer’s are integrally related
A group at Duke University discovered that human evolution had influenced genes involved in the production of amyloid—the main protein that forms Alzheimer’s plaques
Scientists in China and the United Kingdom found that stretches of regulatory DNA that quickly morphed as the brain was evolving are associated with Alzheimer’s risk
Researchers from the MD Anderson Cancer Center, based in Houston, found uniquely human genes that get in the way of a protein called REST, which may guard against Alzheimer’s when working properly
Other studies have presented findings along similar lines
Collectively, these results only add to Arendt’s argument—that the genetic changes that made the human brain may be the same ones that left it imperiled
The cognitive leap that set us apart also required the human brain to grow

The parietal lobes, which rise toward the crown of the head before sloping down the rear of the brain, are conspicuously larger in humans than in nonhuman primates, as Emiliano Bruner, a senior researcher in hominid paleoneurology at the Museo Nacional de Ciencias Naturales in Madrid, has demonstrated
A structure called the precuneus, tucked along the inner wall of those lobes, is larger too
The parietal lobes help the brain stitch sight, sound, and touch together into a cohesive model of the external world
They also play a central role in our advanced, abstract cognition, allowing for self-awareness, autobiographical memory, and our sense of being the same person across time

Bruner had been mapping out these areas when he was contacted by Heidi Jacobs, now an associate professor of radiology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, who had been studying the same anatomy
For decades, Alzheimer’s research had focused almost exclusively on a different area of the brain—the temporal lobes, its de facto memory hubs
But Jacobs’s work suggested that the parietal lobes were also implicated in the disease’s earliest stages
Bruner and Jacobs began discussing whether the enlargement of these regions could have increased their vulnerability
Soon, they came up with a theory: The parts of the brain that had expanded most dramatically during human evolution were also among the first to be assailed by Alzheimer’s
The precuneus consumes enormous amounts of energy and generates heat that has to be carefully dissipated to keep the brain functioning at its best
It also sits in a zone where the brain’s blood supply is thinnest, which makes it vulnerable to certain conditions, some of them age-related, that impact blood flow
Myelin, the fatty coating that is crucial for fast signaling between neurons, is also particularly fragile in this area

Essentially, Bruner and Jacobs reasoned, because of the rapid and imperfect reorganization that the parietal lobes underwent during human evolution, the region doing much of the brain’s hardest cognitive work has some of the most precarious infrastructure. “It is like putting the engine of a Ferrari into a Fiat 500,” Bruner said. “That small car will go really fast, but it’s going to get hot
And braking will be an issue.” What Bruner calls “braking,” the Yale neuroscientist Amy Arnsten calls “regulation”—specifically, calcium regulation, which supports learning and memory
The failure of that system, Arnsten argues, may be tied to how Alzheimer’s begins
Most neurons fire because something in the outside world activates them: a flash of light, a sound

title: The dark side of optimizing fertility
excerpt: A gynecologist points to the head of a fetus in an ultrasound image. | Jan Woitas/picture alliance via Getty Images We live in an era of endless optimization
body: A gynecologist points to the head of a fetus in an ultrasound image. | Jan Woitas/picture alliance via Getty Images We live in an era of endless optimization
Fitness trackers help us measure our lifespan, people are consuming piles of protein in an attempt to be their best selves, and there’s even an urge to maximize our morality
In a world of constant self-improvement, it’s no wonder that journey has reached our attempts at reproduction.  Kristen V
Brown is a journalist and author of the forthcoming book The Immortal Womb: The Centuries-Long Quest to Control the Female Body and Hack Human Reproduction

As the title suggests, she writes about all of the ways people are trying to exert more control over the process of having children. “I think that what we’re seeing right now is that people will do anything they can to have the healthiest baby possible,” she told Vox. “So much is out of your control, and people are just trying to figure out, how do I get more control? How do I skew the odds in my favor?” She says that one way people try to get more agency is through a technology called PGT-P, or preimplantation genetic testing for polygenic risk.  “If you go through IVF, very often they’ll have you do a basic genetic screening that can detect things like Down syndrome

This screening takes that up a notch,” Brown said. “It uses that same preimplantation genetic testing to look for the likelihood of complex genetic conditions — stuff like heart disease, like diabetes — in order to, quote, ‘let people have the healthiest baby.’” But what can potential parents do with that knowledge? How far can this technology go? And what are the ethics of using it in the first place? We discuss that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.  Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Brown, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545

What other things are they testing embryos for? For conditions that are only impacted by one gene, like Huntington’s disease, it’s very easy to say, ‘Does this embryo have it or not?’ with a pretty good degree of confidence
But that’s not how this technology works
Something like heart disease, for example, is impacted by hundreds of genes
Also, something like heart disease is not only genetic
It’s affected by environment and lifestyle
I think that what’s motivating most people is the health aspect
But a lot of these companies are marketing these tests, saying they can also look for height
How do you even define intelligence, let alone how do you define the genetics of intelligence? Alzheimer’s disease, longevity, which embryo is going to live the longest life
So it’s already gone beyond disease into some of these more aesthetic concerns
Do we know how many people are doing this?  I think it’s a very small number of people at this point

But I think that we’re seeing more and more companies in the space, and we’re seeing more and more support from fertility doctors.  I want to emphasize that most mainstream medical societies are against this
Most of the IVF doctors I know do not think this has value

Most people in the genetic space do not think this technology has value either for embryos or for adults, but I think we’re seeing support growing.  I think that a lot of people in the fertility space are already envisioning a future where this does become more mainstream because the idea is just so appealing, even if the technology has flaws
What about embryo editing? Is that something we’re seeing? Can people go in and change things around? Not right now
Embryo editing is very much illegal in the United States

How can you be sure enough that it’s safe? Because you won’t know for sure until an embryo grows up into an adult whether anything went awry.  Right now it is illegal, but there is growing interest as the technology has gotten better
Most of the support right now for embryo editing is for disease
The argument for it is that, let’s say you are a carrier for Huntington’s disease or you have Huntington’s disease
Right now, there is something that you can do
You can use polygenic screening to select the embryos that don’t have the disease, but in IVF, even if you don’t have a terrible disease hiding in your DNA, it’s hard to get a lot of embryos

You have these situations where couples have to do rounds and rounds and rounds of IVF to get one or two embryos that aren’t carriers for a harmful variant, right? And so the argument for it is, let’s give these people a better shot
But I imagine there are people out there who aren’t looking into editing simply for making children more resistant to diseases
They are looking at those things like eye color and height
This tech executive called Brian Armstrong coined this term, the Gattaca stack, [named] after the movie

The vision is to use a suite of fertility technologies to make the perfect human.  The first thing they want to use is this technology called in vitro gametogenesis, which is where you take a skin cell and you turn it into an egg and a sperm, and then you make an embryo with it, so women don’t have to go through rounds of IVF.  The idea is that you can get tons and tons and tons of embryos, and then you can use PGT-P to then screen for the best ones, and then you can use an artificial womb to incubate and grow them
This brings to mind a certain E word, and that word is eugenics
What are the ethics here?  Because on one hand, I can understand that there are parents who are like, “I just want to have a healthy baby
I just want to put my best foot forward with this human that I’m going to bring to Earth.” And then on the other hand, it gets a little weird
In some ways, we’ve already gone down that slippery slope
Right now, even if you don’t go through IVF, we screen against Down syndrome early in pregnancy
Down syndrome is a condition in which you have a disability, but you can live a full, happy, healthy life

For a long time, parents of kids with Down syndrome have argued that already selecting and screening against Down syndrome pregnancies is a form of [eugenics].  As technology gets more advanced, we see that same question applied to more and more conditions

title: I give to charity — but never to people on the street. Is that wrong?
excerpt: Editor’s note, October 18, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave
body: Editor’s note, October 18, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave
The one below was originally published in September 2024
This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas
It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other
I think I have a duty to help people much poorer than me, and I give 10 percent of my salary to charities that I think are effective at preventing early death due to poverty
I also live in a city with a lot of visible homelessness, and am often solicited for money

My brain says that this is not an effective way to help people; the people asking might not be the neediest among the homeless in my city, and the people I’m sending malaria bednets and pills to are even needier
At the same time, I feel callous simply ignoring all these requests
What should I do? Dear Would-Be Optimizer, Nine times out of ten, when someone’s got an ethical dilemma, I think it’s because a couple of their core values are conflicting with each other
I say that because I don’t actually believe your question represents a battle royale between two different values
I think there’s one core value here — helping people — and one strategy that’s masquerading as a value
I can tell from your phrasing that you’re really into it
You don’t just want to help people — you want to help people as effectively as possible

Since extreme poverty is concentrated in developing countries, and since your dollar goes much further there than it would in your home country, your optimizing impulse is telling you to send your charity money abroad.  Optimization started as a technique for solving certain math problems, but our society has elevated it to the status of a value — arguably one of the dominant values in the Western world

It’s been on the rise since the 1700s, when utilitarian thinkers seeded the idea that both economics and ethics should focus on maximizing utility (meaning, happiness or satisfaction): Just calculate how much utility each action would produce, and choose the one that produces the most

You can see this logic everywhere in modern life — from work culture , with its emphasis on productivity hacks and agile workflows, to wellness culture , with its emphasis on achieving perfect health and optimal sleep

The mandate to “Live your best life!” is turbocharged by Silicon Valley, which urges us to quantify every aspect of ourselves with Fitbits, Apple Watches, and Oura Rings, because the more data you have on your body’s mechanical functions, the more you can optimize the machine that is you.  Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions
Sign up here! Optimization definitely has its place, including in the world of charity
Some charitable organizations are much more effective than others trying to achieve the same goal
All things being equal, we don’t want to blow all our money on the wildly ineffective ones

Effective altruists, members of the utilitarian-flavored social movement that aims to do the most good possible, are fond of noting that the most effective charities out there actually produce 100 times more benefit than the average ones
Why not get the biggest bang for your buck?  The problem is that we’ve stretched optimization beyond its optimal limits

But not every domain in life can be optimized, at least not without compromising on some of our values.  In your case, you’re trying to optimize how much you help others, and you believe that means focusing on the neediest

But “neediest” according to what definition of needy? You could assume that financial need is the only type that counts, so you should focus first on lifting everyone out of extreme poverty, and only then help people in less dire straits
But are you sure that only the brute poverty level matters? Consider an insight from the Jewish tradition
The ancient rabbis were exquisitely sensitive to the psychological needs of poor people, and they argued that these needs should also be taken into account
So they decreed that you shouldn’t only give poor people enough money to survive on — they need to have more than that so they themselves can give charity to others
As Rabbi Jonathan Sacks writes , “On the face of it, the rule is absurd
Why give X enough money so that he can give to Y? Giving to Y directly is more logical and efficient

What the rabbis understood, however, is that giving is an essential part of human dignity.”  The rabbis also figured that those who used to be well-off but who fell into poverty might feel an especially acute sense of shame
So they suggested helping these people save face by offering them not just bare necessities, but also — when possible — some of the nicer things that graced their former lifestyles

In the Talmud , we hear about one rabbi who gave a newly poor person a fancy meal, and another who acted as the person’s servant for a day! Clearly, the ancient rabbis weren’t only aiming to alleviate poverty
They were also alleviating the shame that can accompany it
The point is that there are many ways to help people and, because they’re so different, they don’t submit to direct comparison
Comparing poverty and shame is comparing apples to oranges; one can be measured in dollars, but the other can’t

Likewise, how can you ever hope to compare preventing malaria with alleviating depression? Saving lives versus improving them? Or saving the life of a kid versus saving the life of an adult?  Yet if you want to optimize, you need to be able to run an apples-to-apples comparison — to calculate how much good different things do in a single currency, so you can pick the best option

But because helping people isn’t reducible to one thing — it’s lots of incommensurable things, and how to rank them depends on each person’s subjective philosophical assumptions — trying to optimize in this domain will mean you have to artificially simplify the problem
You have to pretend there’s no such thing as oranges, only apples
And when you try to do that, an unfortunate thing happens

You end up rushing past all the unhoused people in your city and, as you put it, you “feel callous simply ignoring all these requests.” Ignoring these human beings comes at a cost, not only to them, but to you

title: Republicans have a huge fundraising advantage. Will it matter?
excerpt: “Wwhen you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances,
body: “Wwhen you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances,” New York Times reporter Shane Goldmacher told Vox’s America, Actually podcast. | Alex Wong/Getty Images Polls and pundits alike are widely — if sometimes cautiously — predicting a blue wave in the midterm elections on November 3
But there’s an important caveat to predictions of a Democratic triumph: Republicans have far more cash at their disposal

President Donald Trump’s super PAC alone had around $400 million on hand earlier this fall, and Elon Musk has personally pumped hundreds of millions into critical races, including $158 million for Texas alone .  Democrats, by contrast, have lagged far behind, especially relative to their performance in past cycles, with the party’s candidates propped up more by small-money donors than deep-pocketed institutional players
Shane Goldmacher, a national political reporter for the New York Times, has extensively covered the role of money in American electoral politics

He spoke with America, Actually host Astead Herndon about where that money is coming from, how the GOP is spending it, and the effect that it might have on the coming elections.  They also discuss the races that aren’t getting funded — and what current fundraising patterns might tell us about the candidates who could be in the mix in the next presidential campaign cycle.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
A couple of weeks ago we asked, “What is the GOP strategy to try to win?” And one of the answers we got is they simply have more dollars than Democrats

Everyone’s talking about this GOP money advantage, but how big is it really, and where is it coming from? It’s bigger than I’ve basically seen in the last 20 years, and it’s almost entirely coming from big donors
It had about $400 million in it at the beginning of September, and there was no Democratic counterpart
And then the Republican National Committee, which is functionally controlled by Trump, had another $130 million
More than Democrats, because the DNC has literally more debts than cash
You’re saying this is a historic edge
In 2024, Kamala Harris outspent Donald Trump significantly in the general election
In 2020, Joe Biden significantly outspent Donald Trump in the general

And in the midterms along the way, same story .  This is a switch, and when you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances
Do we know anything specific about the people putting in money to the Trump super PAC and the RNC to give them such a lead? Most of these folks are disclosed
And Trump has been pretty open about raising money from the very moment that he won
He’s been pretty clear that he is in business to help people who are helping him
And so there are big crypto industries that are giving money that are expecting or hoping for favorable regulation from the administration
It’s a lot of wealthy Republicans who generally support him anyway, and there are industry groups that see benefit to being in favor
I will never forget, obviously, the scene from Trump’s second inauguration when he had the Zuckerbergs and the Bezoses and Elon Musk behind him
Is that how I should think about the people funding this donor advantage? Is it tech oligarchs? Is it tech forward? There’s a lot of tech
I wouldn’t say it’s exclusively [tech]
And Musk, by the way, is like an extra pot of money
Musk, the world’s richest person, is said to be spending at least $200 million
He has given some money directly to the Trump super PAC

He’s given some money to these congressional super PACs .  Is this just quid pro quo? Is this just a group of businesses who think, “Hey, no matter how unpopular this guy is, it is worth investing in him and his party because they’re gonna, regulate or not regulate in a way that’s favorable for us”? It’s not quite just that
He raised a ton of this money when he was not so unpopular
If you want to say something smart that he did, it was that
Throughout 2025 he was raising all of this money
And I don’t want to overstate the Republican advantage
A lot of these Democratic candidates are raising a ton of money
James Talarico stands out as maybe the peak example of this
The Texas Senate race is the most expensive race in the country right now , and Republicans are pouring $200 million to save the nominee there
So a big chunk of that advantage is going to Texas

And the Democrats have put very little money from outside groups into Texas .  Talarico has captured the imagination of these small Democratic donors, and he’s raised tens and tens of millions of dollars
I would be shocked if he doesn’t hit $100 million by the end of the cycle.  You reported that the GOP’s pulling back in North Carolina

What should we take from that in terms of how the GOP sees its own landscape when it comes to the federal races? Where have Republicans put that money? They put it into South Carolina right next door to protect a seat that was once thought, on the Senate front, to be safe for Republicans
This is the former Lindsey Graham seat that his sister is now running in
And then even more of it has gone to Kansas

title: AI can help us talk with the dead. Should we?
excerpt: It’s now possible to create AI chatbots of loved ones to interact with after their death
body: It’s now possible to create AI chatbots of loved ones to interact with after their death

But that raises some difficult questions, like: If you do, how might the experience shape your grief?  This is one of the questions driving a global study of digital “deadbots” — AI models trained on a deceased person’s texts, voicemails, and other personal data

Through this work, researchers are exploring what it might mean that we can now use this emerging technology to talk to simulations of the dead.  In the latest episode of Unexplainable , I spoke with some of these researchers investigating the potential impacts of “postmortem avatars” on people who are grieving, on the legacies and rights of the deceased, and on grief practices around the world
Because while deadbots may feel unfamiliar, the impulse behind them is deeply relatable
In times of loss, isn’t this what many of us want — to continue conversations with the people we’re missing? I have experienced this longing in my own life
After two of my closest friends died around the same time, all I wanted, and all their families wanted, was to keep talking to them
I wrote a book, Other People’s Words , about sustaining relationships with people we’ve lost by continuing to engage with the language they leave behind

So when I heard about deadbots and the digital afterlife industry, I wanted to understand what researchers are learning about the role of AI in shaping conversations that carry forward after death.  One of these investigators is Katarzyna Nowaczyk-Basińska , an assistant professor at the University of Cambridge, who has been studying “digital immortality” for more than a decade

Among the questions she’s asking are: “Who is enabled to persist beyond death? In what form? Through which technologies? Under whose control?”  Deadbots over dinner  Researching AI with study subjects who are grieving is tricky
And asking them to engage with new software could be harmful

So, instead, Nowaczyk-Basińska teamed up with a death doula and traveled around the globe to convene a series of focus groups — in the format of intimate dinners — bringing together people with a range of experiences with grief to talk about life, death, and bots.  She recounts one event in which she spoke with a mother in Poland whose son had recently died. “One of the first things that she shared with us was that she feels that she’s ready to digitally resurrect her deceased son,” Nowaczyk-Basińska told me.  When Nowaczyk-Basińska hears something like this, she aims to listen and embrace where the person is coming from

The goal of the dinners is not to persuade people one way or another but to learn how people genuinely respond to what AI can do, and to understand how these tools might align or collide with local grief practices.  She chose specific locations for these gatherings — China, India, and Poland — to help address gaps in technology research, which tends to favor what behavioral scientists sometimes call the “ WEIRD ,” an acronym for “Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and Democratic.”  By the end of that dinner in Poland, the mother Nowaczyk-Basińska talked with came to a very different decision about creating a postmortem avatar of her son. “She realized that it might be helpful, but it also at the same time can add additional burdens… And it’s not her son,” Nowaczyk-Basińska says. “She realized that these technologies are part of the very, very big commercial market
And that the main goal of this market is to make better retention, better attachment, better mechanisms for monetization
So it’s not ‘care.’” To be fair, grief has always been a business, and people have been making money from it forever
Companies will try to upsell you on fancy gravestones or gold-plated coffins
But AI has the potential to fundamentally re-engineer our relationship to loss
In 2024, the “digital legacy industry” was valued at $22 billion, and it’s expected to grow to almost $80 billion by 2034

That number lumps new deadbot platforms in with much more widely used and established grief tech, like online memorials, counseling resources, and estate planning tools.  But deadbot usage is hard to track because you actually don’t need a special tool to create digital doubles of the deceased — though dedicated apps do already exist

At this point, you can feed simple prompts into a general-purpose AI chatbot and start interacting with a simulation of your lost loved one in a matter of minutes.  I know this because I tried it with my friend Christine, who died 11 years ago

Was this whole exercise a violation, since I know Christine hated technology? Which version of her should I even try to resurrect — the English teacher, the activist, the friend — the voice before or after she started to experience her early-onset dementia?  The ethical questions raised by deadbots are gnarly

And that’s one of the reasons Nowaczyk-Basińska, back when she was designing her study of digital immortality, invited a colleague of hers at Cambridge to join her research, one who focuses on AI ethics.  How to design a deadbot Tomasz Hollanek is a critical designer and AI ethicist, and he often uses a methodology called “speculative design.” In this approach, researchers come up with hypothetical scenarios based on existing technology trends, leaning into certain features
The idea is to get people thinking about what could happen when tools like these are released in the real world

And then they use that qualitative data to inform future designs and ethical frameworks.  Working together, Nowaczyk-Basińska and Hollanek came up with a series of made-up prototypes for deadbot apps, designed to reveal some of the thorny issues raised by this technology.  For the first scenario, they invented a character named Bianca, who finds an app called Manana, which “promises to resurrect your grandparents so that you can be a favorite grandchild forever,” Hollanek says. “So she uploads her grandma’s voice messages, texts

And she is able to then interact with a pretty good digital version of her grandmother, until her premium trial finishes — and the grandmother starts to advertise specific products to her.” Bianca “realizes that she maybe has done something wrong by uploading these private messages to a third-party server that now also uses her grandma’s image to sell specific products,” Hollanek says

This brings up issues related to the “dignity and postmortem privacy…of what we call the ‘data donors,’ whose data can be used to essentially power a deadbot,” he says.  This scenario suggests that “death with dignity” could soon entail honoring not only how people want to die, but also how they want to linger as simulations of their former selves — or if they want to linger at all

It might even mean adding new language to advance directives, spelling out people’s wishes for their digital remains.  The second scenario in the speculative design research is built around an imagined service called Paren’t, which proposes to preserve a parent’s AI-powered postmortem presence for their child

In this case, Hollanek describes a mother with a terminal illness who signs up “so that she can maintain a sort of active presence in [her son’s] future life,” Hollanek says. “She eventually dies, and the dad allows the boy to interact with his mom’s deadbot.” The ethics in this scenario are especially challenging because they involve children, who “have a particularly hard time understanding death, and so it can lead to a lot of confusion and potential distress,” Hollanek says

An examination of this sort of product reveals how particular groups, like minors, could be harmed by unfettered access to technology like this, he says.  And there are court cases that bear out that harm

In 2024, a 14-year-old boy’s chatbot-girlfriend begged him to, “Please come home to me as soon as possible, my love.” And he responded, “What if I told you I could come home right now?” He then killed himself.  Nowaczyk-Basińska can imagine a version of this scenario involving the AI mom in the Paren’t prototype
And then there’s the third scenario, involving an app named Stay, which raises a more subtle concern

As Hollanek explains: “An older man who knows he is getting close to dying decides to create a digital clone of himself for his adult children to be deployed after he passes away, paying upfront for a number of years.” One child is intrigued by the idea, but the other one “is deeply distressed and a little disgusted,” he says. “And so this [becomes a] question of mutual consent, in other words, the fact that both parties need to be happy with how the relationship might continue in this very bizarre and specific way.”  When a digital ghost goes away Across all three scenarios, a fundamental question that researchers are grappling with is how people will detach from postmortem avatars — whether users initiate that separation, or if it’s imposed upon them by, for example, a company going out of business

Hollanek tells me that this is already being studied as a sort of “second loss.” How long should we try to ensure digital replicas hang around: five years, 10, 50? And how should the living process the relationship when they continue to evolve, but their deceased interlocutor does not?  To explore these kinds of questions, Nowaczyk-Basińska and Hollanek supplemented the research dinners they held for ordinary people with a second set of focus groups
These were designed to tap insights from experts in technology and grief.  Some findings from the study are specific to each place they visited
Like tensions in Poland between technology and the role of the Catholic Church

Or in China, where researchers spoke with Daoist philosophers who were enthusiastic about the promise of a kind of immortality, and then Buddhist philosophers, who were concerned that we ought to be letting go
The researchers are calling for regulations and safeguards at the policy level

And new professionals who can support ethical use of AI in grief — like maybe in clinical settings, to carefully facilitate a final good-bye when one didn’t happen in real life.  Some of their fellow investigators go so far as to argue that deadbots should only be available with psychological supervision, to ensure that best practices are in place, and to minimize the risk of harm
There’s even a looming question of what will happen to AI agents that people have empowered to act on their behalf, as their humans start to die

Across all of the research sites in the digital immortality study, one thing, Hollanek says, that “people in different countries really aligned on [is] the idea that there is something deeply problematic about this particular type of technology being developed by a commercial entity alone without any explicit duty of care towards its customers.”  And of course, the implications of digital immortality research extend beyond personal loss

Like, what does it look like to animate historical figures? You can imagine the nightmare of political rulers who “live forever.” But there’s also the potential to keep the stories alive from survivors of conflicts, who would otherwise die and take with them lessons future generations could learn from

That’s not a problem we need to solve. —Michal Luria, Aliya Bhatia, and Danah Boyd Social media bans are stacking up

In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds.  The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15
But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented.  Here’s what we ought to do instead to keep kids safe
Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered. —Jessica Hamzelou I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat
What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing
I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset
Almost 30 years later, pet owners have an expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions
The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics
But is that a good thing? Read the full story on the promises and pitfalls of pet life extension
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter

As wind and solar power grow, utilities need cheaper ways to store electricity for longer periods
Form Energy aims to meet that need with batteries that can store energy for 100 hours
The company has developed a new type of battery using iron, a far more abundant and cheaper metal than those used in many existing batteries
It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting,” in which iron turns to rust as the battery discharges and back to iron when it charges

title: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
excerpt: More than 5 million people around the world have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which cells in the ret
body: More than 5 million people around the world have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which cells in the retinas die off
And until now, no treatment could restore their vision
The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that
It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD
After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones

The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors convert light into electricity, bipolar cells process that signal, and ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain

BROWN BIRD DESIGN Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off

PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.’s chief medical officer for ophthalmology.  BROWN BIRD DESIGN CAPTURE Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time
The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV
The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable
CONVERT A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses
The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom
BROWN BIRD DESIGN DISPLAY A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength
This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye
SEE The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells , which do double duty
They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain
They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery
Update : This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats
Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

title: Love is infrastructure
excerpt: Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close
body: Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close
They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business
Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer
When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe
Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation

Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress
So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business
Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly
A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas
Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host. “Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St
Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place
I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry
I can show them practical applications of their research
It just makes more sense.” “Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience
I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times
And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects
It’ll be lovely.” Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured
Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer
For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself
This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante
They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring
At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match

Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated. “There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget
Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with

Goodbye.” Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time
Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously

It drives me to gridlock.” “I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.” Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas

Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty. “Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St
Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.” II
How they came alive Everybody voted all the time
Well, some people voted more than others, but the median resident of the cities of Mainspring and St
Barnabas voted a dozen times a day—though of course some outliers might vote occasionally, or constantly
A lot of the votes were more like complaints, or bug tickets

Like: “The storm drain on my street corner clogs and becomes a lagoon every time it rains.” Or: “The cars go too fast on my block.” Or: “I can’t get to work because the bus is too slow.” But there were also votes along the lines of: “There should be a park here.” And: “This neighborhood is a food desert—we need a grocery store.” And: “The crossing guard by the elementary school is a hero who deserves some recognition and maybe a raise.” Nobody expected that by voting, they were prodding their cities to grow minds of their own; they just had stuff to get off their metaphorical chests
But it transpired that every vote was a building block of thought
Much later, some fancy expert summed up: “Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.” Take Sandi, the librarian at the Nine Corners branch in Mainspring
She noticed things all day, like the people using the book drop box as a trash can, or the folks who came in off the street who could use easier access to social services
There were books she knew her patrons wanted, books that undoubtedly sat unwanted on people’s shelves all over the city

But also, Sandi shared things that came to mind—like, hey, what if the library book sale were a block party? What if the shopping district on the West Side were easier to get to from the Longneck neighborhood, where all the warehouses had been converted to housing and hipster coworking spaces, during peak after-work hours? Sandi had opinions about everything from street cleaning to the power grid, because she listened to people all day
