title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
excerpt: Pet longevity is a growing area of research: Companies like Loyal are trialing drugs in over 1,300 dogs to combat aging, metabolic disease, and conditions like
body: Pet longevity is a growing area of research: Companies like Loyal are trialing drugs in over 1,300 dogs to combat aging, metabolic disease, and conditions like arthritis — and there's even a longevity medicine company focused entirely on cats

Cloning offers grieving owners "a way to hold on": For $50,000, US company Viagen Pets will create a genetic twin of your dog or cat — not an exact replica, but close enough that some experts see it as a legitimate response to pet loss

Cryonics promises revival, but delivers almost nothing: A handful of companies will freeze your dead pet indefinitely, banking on future technology to bring them back — even those in the field admit reanimation is currently impossible. " data-chronoton-post-id="1146766" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat
I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot
What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing
I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset
There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions
The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics
But is that a good thing? There’s certainly a market for pet preservation
And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity
Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is trialing one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US
Others are testing dog drugs that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like obesity and osteoarthritis , and aging itself
There’s even a company focused on longevity medicines for domesticated cats
But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it
That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though
I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement
In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal
It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing
It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs
In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go
This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin
Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet

On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice
She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets
As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says
Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating
If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?” Fair enough
But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different
It’s often the first time a child confronts death
Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood
I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced
Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics
For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely
The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of
Alcor , a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people
It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider
With cryonics, the chances of being reunited with your pet are bordering on zero
Even those who work in the field acknowledge that the stored people and animals are unlikely to be reanimated
As things stand, there is no way to really and truly bring any animal “back.” I miss Peppy
But given the chance, would I stick her in a vat of liquid nitrogen? Or get another cat to give birth to a genetically identical animal? No, I would not

title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
excerpt: In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by
body: In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds
The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15
But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented
A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms

Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair.  Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds
But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred
The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations
Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence
Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire
Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web
It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age
In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights

That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms.  Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world
At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday
At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world

A less safe internet for kids When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence
It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities
Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online.  It also ignores what some parents want
When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services
This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions
Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care
Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on

Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks.  When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails
Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections
Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation

In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents
Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street
Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them
A less safe internet for all Age gates come with dangers of their own
Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age

In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked.  Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft

Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs

It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences.  Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs

State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court ), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use
But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology
It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation

What could work instead? Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place.  For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children
Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements
Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want
Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable

title: Young voters fear mass shootings like the one in Oregon, but that fear divides them on gun control
url:
<title>Young voters fear mass shootings like the one in Oregon, but that fear divides them on gun control</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766762/original/file-20261016-50-fzfgcm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3977%2C2652&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People leave a family meeting area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15, 2026, in Bend, Ore.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Oregon%20School%20Shooting/83d35196352f423ca913c945621f97bc/photo">AP Photo/Joe Kline</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A gunman shot and killed three children and a teacher at a <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/16/us/live-news/bend-oregon-school-shooting">school in Bend, Oregon</a>, on Oct. 15, 2026, the <a href="https://www.cnn.com/us/school-shootings-fast-facts-dg">52nd school shooting this year</a>, according to CNN. The children’s ages were 5, 8 and 11; a 7-year-old and another teacher were taken to the hospital with critical injuries. The 16-year-old shooting suspect was shot and killed by a bystander.</p>

<p>Though Oregon has <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/us/oregon-gun-control-laws.html">stricter gun laws than most states</a>, some of those laws, such as a measure requiring tougher background checks and requiring a person to have a permit in order to buy a gun, are stalled in court.</p>

<p>The Bend shooting – the latest in a long line of modern school shootings dating back to <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/stockton-massacre/">the late 1980s</a> – comes just weeks before the midterm elections, in which voters will choose members of Congress and state lawmakers who can shape gun laws. </p>

<p>Nearly <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/49-million-young-people-will-be-eligible-vote-2026-midterms">50 million Americans</a> ages 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, and <a href="https://now.tufts.edu/2026/09/22/young-voters-flex-their-power">about 60% say they plan to</a>. If they follow through, it would break midterm turnout records for voters under 30.</p>

<p><a href="https://now.tufts.edu/2026/09/22/young-voters-flex-their-power">Gun control</a> is an issue these young voters care about more than the public at large does, and it’s easy to understand why: In their lifetime, mass shootings have been <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.13148">a recurring part of American life</a>. </p>

<p>Directly experiencing a mass shooting is rare, yet some young people have survived two before turning 25. When a gunman opened fire at Brown University in December 2025, <a href="https://www.thecut.com/article/brown-university-shooting-parkland-survivor.html">at least two students</a> on campus had already experienced a school shooting before they got to college. The same thing happened in April 2025, when students who lived through <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2018/02/15/us/florida-shooting-victims-school">the 2018 Parkland, Florida, shooting</a> at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School found themselves caught in another shooting at <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2025/04/19/us/florida-state-university-shooting-what-we-know">Florida State University</a>. As <a href="https://www.local10.com/news/local/2025/04/17/parkland-school-massacre-survivor-was-at-fsu-during-fatal-shooting/">one of them</a> put it: “This is America.”</p>

<p>Researchers have called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.13148">today’s young adults</a> the “massacre generation.” They’re the first group to grow up entirely in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2019/apr/19/columbine-parkland-how-mass-shootings-changed-us-schools">post-9/11, post-Columbine High School shooting era</a>, with routine <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/fastfacts/display.asp?id=954">lockdown drills</a>, heightened <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/06/the-school-security-industry-was-valued-at-3point1-billion-in-2021.html">security in schools</a> and nonstop <a href="https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/media-exposure-mass-violence-can-fuel-cycle-distress-study-shows">media coverage of mass violence</a>.</p>

<p>As criminologists who study the impacts of <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=cbfYVuoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">victimization and gun violence</a> among <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=X52GgbIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">young people</a>, we wanted to know how growing up with the threat of mass shootings has shaped young adults’ views on gun legislation. In <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.70087">a recent study</a>, we surveyed nearly 1,700 young adults, ages 18 to 29, across the country to find out. We found that fear of mass shootings pulls this generation apart along political and gender lines: It pushes some toward wanting stricter gun laws and others in the opposite direction.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A uniformed law enforcement officer stands behind police tape outside a school building" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766758/original/file-20261016-50-hhpd2f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C438%2C4200%2C2362&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766758/original/file-20261016-50-hhpd2f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766758/original/file-20261016-50-hhpd2f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766758/original/file-20261016-50-hhpd2f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766758/original/file-20261016-50-hhpd2f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766758/original/file-20261016-50-hhpd2f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766758/original/file-20261016-50-hhpd2f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Police tape is placed outside Silver Rail Elementary school, where a shooting took place on Oct. 15, 2026, in Bend, Ore.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/APTOPIX%20Oregon%20School%20Shooting/9d43596a655348c9b084f117f1f97771/photo">AP Photo/Joe Kline</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A debate that repeats after every shooting</h2>

<p>Mass shootings account for <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/04/28/what-the-data-says-about-gun-deaths-in-the-us/">about 1% of gun deaths</a> in the U.S. Still, they profoundly shape how safe millions of Americans feel. In a 2019 <a href="https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/stress/2019/stress-america-2019.pdf">survey by the American Psychological Association</a>, nearly 80% of Americans said the possibility of a mass shooting stressed them out, and a third said they <a href="https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2019/08/fear-mass-shooting">avoided certain places because of it</a>. The fear has become so common that clinicians now have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07481187.2023.2214889">screening tools</a> to assess and treat people with anxiety over mass violence.</p>

<p>Young adults have also grown up watching the same <a href="https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article313732975.html">heated gun debates</a> play out after every tragedy. <a href="https://www.everytown.org/issues/mass-shootings/">Gun control advocates</a> call for <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.12857">stricter firearm restrictions</a> to prevent <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/the-looser-a-states-gun-laws-the-more-mass-shootings-it-has/">the next mass shooting</a>, whereas <a href="https://tpusa.com/live/mass-shootings-are-not-a-reason-for-gun-control/">gun rights advocates</a> push back with the “good guy with a gun” argument, a phrase <a href="https://www.npr.org/2012/12/21/167824766/nra-only-thing-that-stops-a-bad-guy-with-a-gun-is-a-good-guy-with-a-gun">made popular by the National Rifle Association</a>. Supporters of the latter view say more armed citizens are needed to stop active shooters, so more people should be able to buy and carry guns with fewer restrictions, such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.70087">carrying in public without a permit or on college campuses</a>. </p>

<p>Researchers have known for a long time that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/00027162231164865">more guns don’t necessarily mean less violence</a>. A <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07418825.2020.1789693">2021 study</a> found that mass shootings were more common in states with higher rates of gun ownership, and gun homicides were more common in states with looser concealed carry laws. Yet even after <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/390806181_NIJ_Final_Report_A_Comprehensive_Assessment_of_Deadly_Mass_Shootings_1980-2018">decades of mass shootings</a>, federal gun policy has <a href="https://www.bu.edu/articles/2022/the-long-failed-history-of-gun-control-legislation/">barely budged</a>. Even where individual states and local governments have passed assault weapons bans, including <a href="https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/attorney-general-statement-on-scotus-certification-in-challenge-to-connecticut-assault-weapon-ban">Connecticut</a> and <a href="https://www.jurist.org/news/2026/07/us-supreme-court-agrees-to-hear-challenges-to-assault-weapons-bans/">Cook County, Illinois</a>, they’ve faced <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-assault-weapons-debate-is-a-culture-debate-291639">Second Amendment challenges that are now before the Supreme Court</a>.</p>

<p>Young people have become some of the <a href="https://time.com/7304031/march-for-our-lives-pam-bondi-shootings-jaclyn-corin/">loudest voices in this debate</a>, most notably through <a href="https://marchforourlives.org/">March for Our Lives</a> – an organization started by Parkland survivors that focuses on ending gun violence – and <a href="https://www.texastribune.org/2018/06/28/texas-gun-control-high-school-student-activists-santa-fe-mass-shooting/">other youth-led groups</a> across the country. And because pro-gun views tend to be more common among <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/07/24/key-facts-about-americans-and-guns/">older Americans</a>, many political observers assume <a href="https://iop.harvard.edu/press-releases/harvard-iop-youth-poll-finds-stricter-gun-laws-ban-assault-weapons-favored-two">stricter gun laws will follow</a> as young people <a href="https://now.tufts.edu/2026/09/22/young-voters-flex-their-power">gain voting power</a>.</p>

<p>This fall, voters in a few states will weigh in on gun policy directly.</p>

<p>In Massachusetts, voters will decide whether to <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_9,_Firearm_Regulations_Referendum_(2026)">keep or repeal a 2024 law</a> that, among other things, requires gun owners to register their firearms with the state, expands safety training for people applying for a gun license and broadens the state’s ban on assault-style weapons. In Arkansas, they’ll decide whether to <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Arkansas_Issue_2,_Right_to_Keep_and_Bear_Arms_Amendment_(2026)">change the state constitution</a> to more strongly protect gun rights, including the right to own ammunition and gun parts. If young adults turn out in record numbers, their views could help determine outcomes like these.</p>

            </figcaption>

<h2>Young adults are split</h2>

<p>So where do young adults stand? We’ve found that a shared fear of mass shootings does not necessarily lead to shared views on guns. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.70087">Our survey asked</a> young adults to rate on a scale from 1 to 3 – from “not at all” to “a lot” – how much they fear that they or someone they love will become a victim of a mass shooting. More than 60% reported moderate or high levels of fear, including about 17% who fell in the high-fear range.</p>

<p>In general, about two-thirds of young adults said people should need a permit to carry a gun in public and that guns shouldn’t be allowed on college campuses. About 6 in 10 disagreed that owning more guns makes people safer, and a similar share disagreed that gun control laws are unconstitutional.</p>

<p>We found that young adults who worried more about mass shootings tended to be more supportive of gun control. But this pattern didn’t hold for young men, Republicans or those who were politically conservative. For these groups, the opposite was true: The more they feared mass shootings, the less they supported gun restrictions. Young adults are divided on gun control, and those divisions are sharpest when fear runs high. </p>

<p>In the coming years, the massacre generation is on track to become part of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12340">largest voting bloc in the country</a>. Most young adults share a fear of mass shootings, but they disagree on what to do about them. And with each new mass shooting, that divide may only deepen.</p>

<title>Remote work made these colleagues more open with each other, not less</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765671/original/file-20261012-60-gamskh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7360%2C4906&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Many employees see having the freedom to work from home as a benefit.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/black-entrepreneur-wearing-headphones-on-video-royalty-free-image/1369954837?adppopup=true">DigitalVision/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>If you need to participate in video meetings for work, you’ve probably experienced more than one disruption, whether it’s kids darting around or home renovation noise.</p>

<p>Meetings that use Zoom and similar software are a fixture of remote work, which <a href="https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2023/acs/acs-52.html">surged during the COVID-19 pandemic</a> and remains prevalent. As of August 2026, <a href="https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cpseea42.htm">36% of American workers</a> in management, professional and related occupations did at least some of their work from home, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.</p>

<p>I’m a management scholar who studies <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=3I0eCFcAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">how, when and where people work</a>. Before the pandemic began, I was studying a professional services company. That made it possible for me to follow how its staff transitioned from primarily working in person to mostly remote through 2024, which gave me more insight into how remote work has changed people’s lives.</p>

<p>The study included 275 interviews and about 330 hours of observation. Most people in the groups I followed ended up working from home four or five days a week, joining meetings by video. What I found was the opposite of what I expected.</p>



<h2>Learning more about colleagues</h2>

<p>Rather than pulling colleagues apart, remote work brought them closer and made them more willing to be open with one another. The findings were peer-reviewed and will be <a href="https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2024.19818">published in an upcoming issue</a> of the management journal Organization Science.</p>

<p>Before the shift to remote work, I assumed – consistent with the predictions made by many prominent <a href="https://hbr.org/2021/04/what-psychological-safety-looks-like-in-a-hybrid-workplace">researchers of workplace relationships</a> – that moving people out of the office would break down social connections. But I was wrong.</p>

<p>In the office, before the shift to remote work, I found that people primarily viewed one another as work colleagues rather than whole people. Reflecting this relationship, workers sometimes said they felt uncomfortable sharing with one another aspects of their lives that might limit their ability to do work.</p>

<p>For example, one worker I interviewed, Patrick, was afraid to tell his colleagues he could not work late one night because he was helping his mom. All the names I’m mentioning are pseudonyms to protect the privacy of the people involved and their employer.</p>

<p>“Even though you didn’t sleep last night, you’re expected to show up and smile and be fine,” said Tamara, an exhausted parent with two young children, when she was still commuting regularly to the office.</p>

<p>Surprisingly, people told me that they learned a lot more about one another once they began to work remotely instead of being together in an office. During my research, I heard about children yelling in the background and pets wandering in front of cameras. A spouse arriving home from work stopped to say hello on screen. </p>

<p>In team chat channels, people posted photos of their children, their animals and the meals they had cooked.</p>

<p>“Everyone has noises in the background, or they have something going on or whatever, and so we get to know each other quicker and on a deeper level than we would otherwise,” Tamara told me. In some cases, this increased sense of closeness happened to people who had known each other for years prior to switching to remote work.  </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765674/original/file-20261012-50-7stz3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Woman works from home with a candlestick chart on laptop and cat on her desk." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765674/original/file-20261012-50-7stz3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765674/original/file-20261012-50-7stz3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765674/original/file-20261012-50-7stz3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765674/original/file-20261012-50-7stz3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765674/original/file-20261012-50-7stz3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765674/original/file-20261012-50-7stz3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765674/original/file-20261012-50-7stz3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">When you’re a remote employee, you may get more quality time with your pets.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-working-from-home-with-candlestick-chart-on-royalty-free-image/2210727461?adppopup=true">Moment/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Growing psychological safety</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-031413-091305">Psychological safety</a> is the sense that you can take an interpersonal risk at work, such as admitting a mistake, asking for help or raising a problem, without being judged negatively.</p>

<p>Decades of management research tie psychological safety to important outcomes for both workers and organizations, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-120920-055217">learning, creativity and speaking up</a>.</p>

<p>Over time, working remotely seemed to improve psychological safety for many of these co-workers.</p>

<p>People became “less afraid to talk about the interface of their personal and professional lives,” Leah said. Before, she added, no one would have volunteered that a breakup was affecting them and that they needed a day off to decompress.</p>

<p>After the company went remote, people told me they felt more comfortable sharing their own challenges as they tried to juggle their work and the challenges they faced in their personal lives.</p>

<h2>Supporting work and nonwork activities</h2>

<p>And as people started sharing these problems with their co-workers, they also told me they felt as if they could then better support one another.</p>

<p>When one worker’s father fell ill, his colleague, Brooke, took over the tasks the two had planned to do together. </p>

<p>“I’m just going to take this over for you right now,” Brooke told him. “And then, whenever you can, come back and swoop in.”</p>

<p>The colleague was able to dedicate time to caring for his father. And importantly, because help circulated this way, Brooke said, a task no longer “stopped dead in the water” when one person could not get to it.</p>

<p>This deeper collaboration did not seem to come at the expense of getting tasks completed. As an employee I’m calling Charles explained, having co-workers sharing details about their personal lives has “helped us to work more effectively in a lot of ways.”</p>

<p>Crucially, these improvements were experienced by people with many different living arrangements – young and old, those with and without kids or partners, men and women. And these benefits were positively reinforcing. For instance, sharing more meant learning more about others, which further reinforced psychological safety.</p>

<p>My findings suggest that remote work can be a benefit that employers and employees may overlook. Rather than treating time out of the office as a cost to social connection among employees, they might treat it as a way to grow personally and get to know co-workers better.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291728/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Over time, working remotely seemed to improve psychological safety for many of these co-workers
People became “less afraid to talk about the interface of their personal and professional lives,” Leah said
Before, she added, no one would have volunteered that a breakup was affecting them and that they needed a day off to decompress
After the company went remote, people told me they felt more comfortable sharing their own challenges as they tried to juggle their work and the challenges they faced in their personal lives
Supporting work and nonwork activities And as people started sharing these problems with their co-workers, they also told me they felt as if they could then better support one another

When one worker’s father fell ill, his colleague, Brooke, took over the tasks the two had planned to do together. “I’m just going to take this over for you right now,” Brooke told him. “And then, whenever you can, come back and swoop in.” The colleague was able to dedicate time to caring for his father
And importantly, because help circulated this way, Brooke said, a task no longer “stopped dead in the water” when one person could not get to it
This deeper collaboration did not seem to come at the expense of getting tasks completed

As an employee I’m calling Charles explained, having co-workers sharing details about their personal lives has “helped us to work more effectively in a lot of ways.” Crucially, these improvements were experienced by people with many different living arrangements – young and old, those with and without kids or partners, men and women
And these benefits were positively reinforcing
For instance, sharing more meant learning more about others, which further reinforced psychological safety
My findings suggest that remote work can be a benefit that employers and employees may overlook
Rather than treating time out of the office as a cost to social connection among employees, they might treat it as a way to grow personally and get to know co-workers better

<title>Belonging and belief: Why evangelical churches draw many migrants in the US</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766547/original/file-20261015-50-c4nx4m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People pray during a service in a storefront church in the Little Havana neighborhood of Miami, Fla.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/louis-enrique-originally-from-nicaragua-prays-during-a-news-photo/76043617?phrase=evangelical%20church%20immigrant%20u.s.&amp;adppopup=true">Joe Raedle/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In October 2024, right before the presidential election, I had coffee with Kim, a Congolese asylum-seeker living in southern Maine. Our conversation quickly turned to politics, and I cautiously asked about her views, although she could not vote.</p>

<p>During his campaign, Donald Trump <a href="https://www.npr.org/2024/10/30/nx-s1-5170339/trumps-mass-deportation-plan-of-undocumented-migrants-offers-few-specifics">had vowed mass deportations</a>, and I assumed immigration policies would be among her top priorities. </p>

<p>But instead, she quickly turned to matters of faith, invoking her strongly held beliefs. Kim – a pseudonym, like all names used in this article – was an evangelical Christian whose life revolved around her church: a nondenominational congregation led by other Congolese migrants. </p>

<p>“Democrats are not people of God,” she declared. People in her community were “traditional,” she added, and generally wanted politicians who were, too. Congolese Christians, she said, usually believed marriage should only occur between a man and a woman, that sex and gender are chosen by God, and that life is sacred from conception.</p>

<p>Her pronouncement underscores an important but often overlooked reality. Popular commentary in the U.S. often portrays evangelicals as one homogeneous, overwhelmingly white group. In reality, they are diverse, from political views and geography to race: <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/age-race-education-and-other-demographic-traits-of-us-religious-groups/">3 in 10 U.S. evangelicals are not</a> white.</p>

<p>And <a href="https://www.christianitytoday.com/2024/02/evangelical-immigration-reform-lifeway-safety-threat-econom/">a growing percentage</a> are migrants – a term I use for people who have come to the U.S., regardless of their legal status.</p>

<h2>Belonging and belief</h2>

<p>Overall, 12% of evangelicals in the U.S. were born outside the country, <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/age-race-education-and-other-demographic-traits-of-us-religious-groups/#immigration-and-region-of-birth">according to a 2024 study</a> conducted by the Pew Research Center. Another 7% have at least one parent born outside the country. These figures are likely underestimates, since undocumented migrants generally avoid surveys for fear of deportation.</p>

<p>As an <a href="https://www.johannarichlin.com/">anthropologist of religion</a>, I’ve studied the growing number of migrants drawn to evangelical faith – and learned how significantly faith shapes their lives in the United States. In turn, these migrants are <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/rowman--littlefield-handbook-of-contemporary-christianity-in-the-united-states-9781538196434/">shaping America’s religious landscape</a>. </p>

<p>While writing my 2022 book, “<a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691194981/in-the-hands-of-god?srsltid=AfmBOooJMOdCYZBsIP6VCmLVMnZ1SEBZA7uAl2xB81__agiw2ZDFkihU">In the Hands of God</a>,” I spent over a year attending evangelical churches around Washington, D.C., that catered to Brazilian migrants. I interviewed about 80 churchgoers and surveyed dozens more. </p>

<p>Congregants described how belief and belonging helped them overcome challenges such as loneliness, “feeling stuck” due to their legal precariousness and being exploited at work. I heard stories of employers holding migrants’ passports hostage, or refusing to pay construction workers seriously injured on the job.</p>

<p>Migrants often told me that their churches’ close-knit communities, and evangelical Christianity’s emphasis on fostering an intimate relationship with God, <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/26854758">gave them a sense of empowerment</a>. Through prayer, worship, Bible study and fasting, they tried to discern and implement God’s plan for their lives. </p>

<p>The three congregations that I attended offered multiple prayer, study and worship opportunities for migrants throughout the week, both at church and at congregants’ homes. Many pastors were migrants themselves and shared from the pulpit their stories of overcoming adversity. </p>

<p>Gláucia, an undocumented migrant from Brazil, described leaving herself “in the hands of God” as she faced uncertainty about her future. </p>

<p>“I love living here,” she explained. “But if God wants me to leave, I’m under God’s will. Wherever God directs me, I will go. Therefore, I don’t get worried, because we can’t become worried about what comes tomorrow. Because tomorrow belongs to God.</p>

<p>"The most I can do,” she added, “which I always try to do, is pray to God to give direction” to political leaders. </p>

<h2>Growing communities</h2>

<p>Some people I met identified as evangelical before coming to the U.S., but a significant number were converts. Even among people who had attended evangelical churches in Brazil, many insisted that they truly “met Jesus” in the United States and reflected that their faith back home had been “lukewarm.”</p>

<p>Angela, an undocumented migrant, knew many evangelicals in Brazil. It wasn’t until arriving in the U.S., though, that she converted from Catholicism. She told me, “When you are here, without your family, without any friends, you feel alone, and look for something to hold on to,” she told me. </p>

<p>According to large-scale surveys, <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2013/05/17/the-religious-affiliation-of-us-immigrants/">most immigrants in the U.S. are Christian</a>, and <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3629734/">the majority of Christian migrants are Catholic</a>.</p>

<p>Over the past several decades, however, a growing percentage of people in Latin America, long a Catholic stronghold, <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2014/11/13/religion-in-latin-america/">have been embracing evangelical churches</a>. That has influenced the religious makeup of migrants to the United States. Others convert to evangelical Christianity <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691194981/in-the-hands-of-god?srsltid=AU7gw4VwLjQ6Py74sgZV5QzvMGf1gY-dNFjzbKwU3O2dQ6RbECgptcja">once they arrive</a>, as my research highlights.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Most of the migrants I met reported intense psychological pain as they endured  family separation, workplace exploitation and legal uncertainty, which prompted them to search for meaning and comfort in religious spaces. Migrant evangelical churches, they found, <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/26854758">spoke directly to their distress</a>. Their style of worship and theological teachings provided concrete tools, including practices such as prayer, fasting and sharing personal testimony, that relieved migrants’ suffering.</p>

<p>Research suggests it is also common for migrants from other parts of the world, <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691164663/getting-saved-in-america">including Taiwan</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/3711910">and China</a>, to turn to evangelical, charismatic and Pentecostal churches to address difficulties <a href="https://www.rutgersuniversitypress.org/a-place-to-be/9780813544939">they confront in the United States</a>.</p>

<h2>Changing face of Christianity</h2>

<p>Evangelical churches play a major role in these migrants’ experiences of the U.S. In turn, these migrants are playing a significant role in American Christianity, as I explain in “<a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/rowman--littlefield-handbook-of-contemporary-christianity-in-the-united-states-9781538196434/">The Handbook of Contemporary Christianity in the United States</a>.”  </p>

<p>Over the past few decades, Americans have become <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/decline-of-christianity-in-the-us-has-slowed-may-have-leveled-off/#trends-in-the-religiousness-of-christians">less Christian and less religious</a>. In 2007, 78% of Americans called themselves Christians; today, that number is 63%. </p>

<p>Migrants, however, are <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/2024/08/19/geographic-spotlights-a-closer-look-at-4-migration-stories/">more likely to have a religious affiliation</a>: 87%, compared with 70% of all people in the United States. In Maine, for example, where I live, journalists have noted how <a href="https://www.mainepublic.org/arts-and-culture/2024-06-13/african-immigration-to-maine-fuels-boom-in-new-churches-bringing-distinct-forms-of-christianity">African migrants are reinvigorating churches</a>. And many <a href="https://www.patheos.com/blogs/anxiousbench/2021/09/the-2020-census-immigration-and-the-future-of-american-evangelicalism/">thriving migrant churches are evangelical</a>.</p>

<p>Looking toward the future, I believe these trends will continue to transform U.S. religion, which may affect politics as well. Many migrants I met, including green-card holders and asylum-seekers, hoped to eventually gain citizenship and be able to vote. Many attended church alongside their own children, born in the U.S. – future voters whose attitudes may be shaped by their parents’ experiences of both migration and faith.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>I learned that evangelical migrants’ identity as “people of God” was central to their political views, as it is for their white, U.S.-born counterparts. Some of them believed Trump would restore the United States to its presumed destiny as an explicitly Christian nation. His policies about abortion, marriage and gender seemed to outweigh concerns about the risks his immigration policies posed to them and their families. Since the start of his second term, with its waves of <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/01/16/nx-s1-5675286/violent-incidents-involving-ice-raise-questions-about-their-training-and-use-of-force">sometimes violent</a> and aggressive <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/25/us/ice-surge-immigration-arrests.html">ICE raids</a>, detentions and deportations, I have wondered how they would assess the administration today.</p>

<p>Regardless of their political views, it is clear that migrants will continue to look to evangelical faith to cope with and make sense of their experiences in the United States. My research underscores the significant role evangelical faith plays in the life of growing numbers of migrants and the far-reaching impacts of such faith for U.S. society.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/286504/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Congregants described how belief and belonging helped them overcome challenges such as loneliness, “feeling stuck” due to their legal precariousness and being exploited at work
I heard stories of employers holding migrants’ passports hostage, or refusing to pay construction workers seriously injured on the job
Migrants often told me that their churches’ close-knit communities, and evangelical Christianity’s emphasis on fostering an intimate relationship with God, gave them a sense of empowerment
Through prayer, worship, Bible study and fasting, they tried to discern and implement God’s plan for their lives
The three congregations that I attended offered multiple prayer, study and worship opportunities for migrants throughout the week, both at church and at congregants’ homes
Many pastors were migrants themselves and shared from the pulpit their stories of overcoming adversity

Gláucia, an undocumented migrant from Brazil, described leaving herself “in the hands of God” as she faced uncertainty about her future. “I love living here,” she explained. “But if God wants me to leave, I’m under God’s will
Therefore, I don’t get worried, because we can’t become worried about what comes tomorrow
Because tomorrow belongs to God. "The most I can do,” she added, “which I always try to do, is pray to God to give direction” to political leaders
Members of the First Brazilian Church of Boston pray during a Sunday evening service in 2013
Kelvin Ma/MediaNews Group/Boston Herald via Getty Images Growing communities Some people I met identified as evangelical before coming to the U.S., but a significant number were converts

Even among people who had attended evangelical churches in Brazil, many insisted that they truly “met Jesus” in the United States and reflected that their faith back home had been “lukewarm.” Angela, an undocumented migrant, knew many evangelicals in Brazil
It wasn’t until arriving in the U.S., though, that she converted from Catholicism
She told me, “When you are here, without your family, without any friends, you feel alone, and look for something to hold on to,” she told me
According to large-scale surveys, most immigrants in the U.S. are Christian , and the majority of Christian migrants are Catholic
Over the past several decades, however, a growing percentage of people in Latin America, long a Catholic stronghold, have been embracing evangelical churches
That has influenced the religious makeup of migrants to the United States
Others convert to evangelical Christianity once they arrive , as my research highlights
People attend Sunday services at the Church of Grace to Fujianese in New York in 2010

Najlah Feanny/Corbis via Getty Images Most of the migrants I met reported intense psychological pain as they endured family separation, workplace exploitation and legal uncertainty, which prompted them to search for meaning and comfort in religious spaces

<title>Treating depression during pregnancy may benefit baby’s brain development – new research</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764039/original/file-20261006-50-sc67av.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6720%2C4480&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Depression affects 1 in 5 women during pregnancy. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/pregnant-woman-receiving-emotional-support-during-royalty-free-image/2229743179">SDI Productions/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Treating pregnant women’s depression with a short course of talk therapy doesn’t just improve their health – it can also shape <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78276-4">how their babies’ brains develop before birth</a>. That’s the finding of a new study we co-authored, published in the journal Nature Communications.  </p>

<p>The study is part of <a href="https://careprojectdenver.org/">an ongoing research project</a> that explores how a form of brief interpersonal psychotherapy called MOMCare, which is specially tailored to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/da.22405">treating prenatal depression</a>, affects pregnant women with depression and their babies. MOMCare consists of eight 50-minute sessions focused on building interpersonal skills, reducing conflict and strengthening social support. </p>

<p>We enrolled 234 pregnant women who reported having symptoms of depression during their routine prenatal care appointments. Mothers joined the research project during the first or second trimester and were randomly assigned to one of two groups. </p>

<p>Women in one group received MOMCare. Women in the other group received education about mental health, strategies for managing depression symptoms and referrals to mental health support services, such as therapy, in the community. Both groups continued getting their usual medical care, which could also include referrals to therapy or medication.</p>

<p>In a previous publication, we found that 36% of moms enrolled in our study were diagnosed with depression in pregnancy before getting MOMCare and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2023.0702">just 6% after it</a>, showing the intervention was effective. Women who received the MOMCare intervention were also more likely to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eclinm.2024.102601">carry their baby to term</a>, which is linked with shorter hospital stays after birth and improvements in many aspects of child health and development, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2020.2027">better school performance</a>. </p>

<p>In the current study, to investigate how this form of talk therapy affects a baby’s developing brain, we measured the volume of different brain areas using an imaging technique called <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/4876-magnetic-resonance-imaging-mri">magnetic resonance imaging</a>, or MRI, within a few weeks of birth. We found that a brain area called the <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/hippocampus">hippocampus</a>, which plays a role in learning, memory and <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-emotional-regulation-a-child-psychologist-explains-280443">emotional regulation</a>, was 5% smaller by volume in infants whose mothers received MOMCare compared to mothers in the other group. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A baby in a high chair playing with an educational block toy" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Brain imaging showed a difference in the brains of newborns whose moms got talk therapy compared to those whose moms who did not.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/asian-baby-boy-develops-fine-motor-skills-playing-royalty-free-image/2232215754">travelism/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>



<p>Six months later, we brought the babies back into the lab to examine their emotional responses to unfamiliar experiences, such as encountering a noisy toy robot that danced and moved unpredictably. According to earlier studies, babies who respond more negatively to these tasks have higher levels of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/abn0000769">depression and anxiety</a> in adolescence. </p>

<p>In our study, we found that babies with a smaller hippocampal volume at birth tended to respond less negatively than those with larger volume. </p>

<p>It may seem counterintuitive that a smaller brain volume is associated with stronger emotional regulation, particularly since in adults smaller brain volume is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nn958">often associated with negative effects</a>. However, in infancy the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2024.101392">brain is growing</a>, and faster growth may not always be advantageous. For example, one hypothesis proposes that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cobeha.2015.11.018">stress can accelerate early brain development</a>. </p>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>Depression affects up to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2021.00615">1 in 5 women during pregnancy</a>. It also raises the risk of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/archgenpsychiatry.2010.111">pregnancy complications</a> such as high blood pressure and preterm birth. And having depression during pregnancy raises the risk of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lanepe.2026.101595">mental illness in the child</a>. </p>

<p>Pregnancy offers a unique opportunity to simultaneously improve the health of both mother and baby. This is because women often have more contact with the healthcare system during pregnancy than at other times in their lives. Treating a woman’s depression during her pregnancy benefits <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0954579418000470">two generations</a>, improving the health of the mother and her developing baby. </p>

<p>Even though both MOMCare and the control condition in our study provided more support than pregnant women experiencing symptoms of depression often receive, we still saw a big difference between the groups. This suggests that a targeted intervention, even a noninvasive and relatively low-cost one such as MOMCare, can make a big difference. </p>

<p>Our study is the first to show that treating a woman’s depression during pregnancy may influence infant brain development. It aligns with a small but growing number of randomized clinical trials showing that reducing maternal depression has benefits for babies, including improved <a href="https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.1222-12693R3">emotional development</a> and changes in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssmmh.2022.100082">stress-related hormones</a>.</p>

<p>These findings, if confirmed, could explain the biological underpinnings behind why treating prenatal depression is so critical. Further, they support public health initiatives to increase <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cct.2025.107988">accessible mental health support</a> during pregnancy. </p>

<h2>What’s still unknown</h2>

<p>It’s not clear how lessening mom’s depression in pregnancy leads to changes in the baby’s brain. It’s possible, for example, that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.psyneuen.2016.10.005">stress-related hormones</a> or <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291719001909">inflammation associated with depression</a> could influence brain growth.</p>

<p>Another open question is how the brain changes we observed might affect babies’ development long term. We hope to address this by continuing to follow mothers and babies through early childhood. By tracking conditions such as depression and anxiety as the children get older, we hope to determine whether treating mothers’ depression in pregnancy has lasting benefits for their children’s mental health and well-being.</p>

title: Fentanyl is fueling overdose deaths in Colorado – what voters need to know about Proposition 132’s attempt to stiffen penalties
url:
<title>Fentanyl is fueling overdose deaths in Colorado – what voters need to know about Proposition 132’s attempt to stiffen penalties</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763959/original/file-20261005-50-zotpy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5616%2C3744&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Fentanyl-related overdose deaths are a concern in Colorado.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/drug-grams-and-tabs-royalty-free-image/482857483?phrase=group%20of%20people%20fentanyl&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm">KatarzynaBialasiewicz/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Colorado continues to face an increase in overdose deaths while other states have seen a downturn.</p>

<p>Illicitly manufactured fentanyl, a potent opioid, emerged in the Colorado drug market around 2018. That was nearly five years after it began tormenting people who use street drugs in <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.15585/mmwr.mm6614a2">Northeastern states</a>. </p>

<p>By 2019, fentanyl replaced other drugs as the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/drug-overdose-data.htm">driving force behind opioid overdoses in Colorado</a>, and it has <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/drug-overdose-data.htm">held its grip</a> ever since.</p>

<p>But while <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/drug-overdose-data.htm">overdose deaths in the U.S.</a> are currently experiencing a historic decline of almost 14%, Colorado is <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/5878575-drug-overdose-deaths-declined-last-year-except-in-these-8-states/">one of eight states where rates are not dropping</a>. In fact, Colorado has had an increase of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/drug-overdose-data.htm">nearly 12% in overdose deaths</a> since April 2025. </p>

<p>Overdoses are top of mind for many everyday Coloradans, healthcare professionals, elected officials and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=WaGmzxoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">public health experts like me</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_132,_Penalties_for_Fentanyl_Sale_and_Possession_Initiative_(2026)">Proposition 132</a> attempts to address these concerns by stiffening legal penalties. A conservative policy organization called Advance Colorado collected the signatures to get the initiative on the November ballot.</p>

<p>The proposed change to Colorado law would make possession of any amount of fentanyl a felony, require a mandatory minimum eight-year prison sentence for distribution of any quantity of fentanyl, and eliminate some existing opportunities for reduced penalties. </p>

<p>Before Coloradans head to the polls, it is worth examining the state’s overdose trends and considering whether Proposition 132 is likely to solve the problem.</p>

<h2>A 2022 law already increased penalties</h2>

<p>Let’s start by looking at Colorado’s past attempts to stop drug overdoses through legislation.</p>

<p>In recent years, the state has pursued some public health interventions but has leaned heavily on increasing criminal penalties for using and possessing fentanyl. </p>

<p>The 2022 <a href="https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb22-1326">Fentanyl Accountability and Prevention Act (HB22-1326)</a>, for instance, represented a major expansion of criminal penalties.</p>

<p>This law rolled back a <a href="https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb19-1263">2019 law</a> that had decriminalized small amounts of drugs. Specifically, HB22-1326 made the knowing possession of more than 1 gram and up to 4 grams of a <a href="https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb22-1326">substance containing fentanyl a Level 4 drug felony</a> punishable by up to 180 days in jail and two years of probation. </p>

<p>Unlike Proposition 132, the 2022 fentanyl act directed funding for the distribution of naloxone, an overdose reversal medication, and fentanyl test strips that help people identify fentanyl in their drugs before using them. Both <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.f174">naloxone</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.10077">fentanyl test strips</a> decrease the risk of fatal overdose. </p>

<p>The law did not direct funding toward evidence-based treatments such as methadone or buprenorphine for <a href="https://nida.nih.gov/research-topics/medications-opioid-use-disorder#buprenorphine">opioid use disorder</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://patch.com/colorado/across-co/fentanyl-accountability-prevention-bill-moves-governors-desk">Supporters argued</a> that the legislation was necessary to prevent overdose deaths and get people treatment.</p>

<p>I led a research team that included addiction treatment providers and substance use–focused epidemiologists to study the effects of HB22-1326. Although more people were arrested and faced the tougher penalties, we found <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.drugpo.2025.105037">no increase in people beginning or staying on buprenorphine</a>. We also found that fewer people were starting and staying on methadone following the implementation of the law. </p>

<p>Importantly, we found that the law did not change <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamahealthforum.2025.2654">the trajectory of overdose deaths</a> compared to what was expected. Taken together, we found no substantial evidence that increasing criminal penalties, even with some increased funding for naloxone and overdose prevention, “saved lives” as proponents had hoped. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Top view of youth talking with a therapist while sitting in a circle during a meeting." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">In addition to increased criminalization, Colorado has invested in prevention programs and treatment support for users of illicit drugs.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/top-view-on-difficult-youth-talking-with-therapist-royalty-free-image/1007209056">KatarzynaBialasiewicz/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Colorado is already <a href="https://www.networkforphl.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/State-Fentanyl-Penalty-Enhancements_A-Comprehensive-Legal-Review-2.pdf">uniquely punitive toward people who use illicit drugs</a>, with some of the harshest penalties for drug possession and distribution in the U.S. Colorado’s public health response has developed alongside, not in place of, a substantial criminal-legal response.</p>

<h2>What decreases overdose deaths?</h2>

<p>Even with <a href="https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/HB24-1037">efforts to provide additional access to harm-reduction protections</a>, escalating criminal penalties have not produced the treatment gains or decreases in overdose deaths in Colorado that proponents promised. </p>

<p>So, let’s look at a place in the state where overdose deaths are actually falling to see what is being done differently there. </p>

<p>Larimer County, home of Colorado State University and part of Rocky Mountain National Park, offers the clearest contrast to the rest of the state. Accidental overdose deaths <a href="https://cohealthviz.dphe.state.co.us/t/HealthInformaticsPublic/views/Drug_Overdose_Dashboard_All_Years_No_Race_FINAL/Story1">have declined year after year since 2022</a>, down nearly 42% from 2021.</p>

<p>What’s going on in Larimer County?</p>

<p>For one, the Larimer County Jail is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s40352-026-00434-z">one of less than half</a> of the Colorado county jails that offers  that includes medications for opioid use disorder. </p>

<p>The sheriff’s office, in collaboration with several community-based organizations, has also flooded the community with naloxone through the <a href="https://www.larimer.gov/spotlights/2024/01/29/grant-fuels-battle-against-opioid-crisis-repeat-offenses">Reversal Project</a>. Furthermore, <a href="https://www.larimer.gov/bocc/regional-opioid-abatement-council#docaccess-d2eae7271383f0388efc8934636fbb8d">using opioid abatement funds</a>, the county has expanded youth and family support services, co-responder units and other harm-reduction services. The county has also steadily <a href="https://cohealthviz.dphe.state.co.us/t/PSDVIP-MHPPUBLIC/views/BuprenorphineDashboard/BupeNaive?%3Aembed=y&amp;%3AisGuestRedirectFromVizportal=y&amp;%3Aorigin=card_share_link">increased the number of people on buprenorphine</a>. </p>

<p>No single intervention can be credited with Larimer County’s decline in accidental overdoes deaths. Criminal enforcement remains one component of the county’s response. Yet, what stands out is its emphasis on evidence-based interventions with an emphasis on expanding treatment access and harm-reduction services that save lives and give people the stability and opportunity to build healthier lives. </p>

<h2>A polysubstance problem</h2>

<p>In addition, Proposition 132 has a major flaw. It targets one drug: fentanyl. </p>

<p>But the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/overdose-prevention/data-research/facts-stats/sudors-dashboard-fatal-overdose-data.html">available data suggests</a> most people take fentanyl together with stimulants such as methamphetamine. Both drugs can be fatal.</p>

<p>Between 2020 and 2024, nearly 40% of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/overdose-prevention/data-research/facts-stats/sudors-dashboard-fatal-overdose-data.html">overdose deaths in Colorado</a> involved both opioids and stimulants. </p>

<p>National figures follow a similar pattern. Nationally, 43% of overdose deaths in 2024 <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/overdose-prevention/data-research/facts-stats/sudors-dashboard-fatal-overdose-data.html">involved both opioids and stimulants</a>. </p>

<p>Targeting one substance, as Proposition 132 does, ignores the fact that the state has a true “polysubstance” epidemic and will end up making people who unknowingly possess fentanyl susceptible to harsher penalties set forth by Proposition 132.</p>

<p>Since Colorado increased fentanyl penalties in 2022, the promised treatment gains examined in our research have not materialized. The state’s number of overdoses has continued to climb.</p>

<p>Those facts do not mean that criminal penalties alone caused Colorado’s worsening trend. But they do raise an important question as voters consider Proposition 132: What evidence suggests that increasing those penalties further will address the rise in overdose deaths?</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292870/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Fentanyl-related overdose deaths are a concern in Colorado
KatarzynaBialasiewicz/iStock via Getty Images Plus Colorado continues to face an increase in overdose deaths while other states have seen a downturn
Illicitly manufactured fentanyl, a potent opioid, emerged in the Colorado drug market around 2018
That was nearly five years after it began tormenting people who use street drugs in Northeastern states
By 2019, fentanyl replaced other drugs as the driving force behind opioid overdoses in Colorado , and it has held its grip ever since
But while overdose deaths in the U.S. are currently experiencing a historic decline of almost 14%, Colorado is one of eight states where rates are not dropping
In fact, Colorado has had an increase of nearly 12% in overdose deaths since April 2025
Overdoses are top of mind for many everyday Coloradans, healthcare professionals, elected officials and public health experts like me
Proposition 132 attempts to address these concerns by stiffening legal penalties
A conservative policy organization called Advance Colorado collected the signatures to get the initiative on the November ballot

The proposed change to Colorado law would make possession of any amount of fentanyl a felony, require a mandatory minimum eight-year prison sentence for distribution of any quantity of fentanyl, and eliminate some existing opportunities for reduced penalties
Before Coloradans head to the polls, it is worth examining the state’s overdose trends and considering whether Proposition 132 is likely to solve the problem
A 2022 law already increased penalties Let’s start by looking at Colorado’s past attempts to stop drug overdoses through legislation
In recent years, the state has pursued some public health interventions but has leaned heavily on increasing criminal penalties for using and possessing fentanyl
The 2022 Fentanyl Accountability and Prevention Act (HB22-1326) , for instance, represented a major expansion of criminal penalties
This law rolled back a 2019 law that had decriminalized small amounts of drugs

Specifically, HB22-1326 made the knowing possession of more than 1 gram and up to 4 grams of a substance containing fentanyl a Level 4 drug felony punishable by up to 180 days in jail and two years of probation

Unlike Proposition 132, the 2022 fentanyl act directed funding for the distribution of naloxone, an overdose reversal medication, and fentanyl test strips that help people identify fentanyl in their drugs before using them
Both naloxone and fentanyl test strips decrease the risk of fatal overdose
The law did not direct funding toward evidence-based treatments such as methadone or buprenorphine for opioid use disorder
Supporters argued that the legislation was necessary to prevent overdose deaths and get people treatment
I led a research team that included addiction treatment providers and substance use–focused epidemiologists to study the effects of HB22-1326
Although more people were arrested and faced the tougher penalties, we found no increase in people beginning or staying on buprenorphine
We also found that fewer people were starting and staying on methadone following the implementation of the law
Importantly, we found that the law did not change the trajectory of overdose deaths compared to what was expected
Taken together, we found no substantial evidence that increasing criminal penalties, even with some increased funding for naloxone and overdose prevention, “saved lives” as proponents had hoped
In addition to increased criminalization, Colorado has invested in prevention programs and treatment support for users of illicit drugs

KatarzynaBialasiewicz/iStock via Getty Images Plus Colorado is already uniquely punitive toward people who use illicit drugs , with some of the harshest penalties for drug possession and distribution in the U.S
Colorado’s public health response has developed alongside, not in place of, a substantial criminal-legal response

What decreases overdose deaths? Even with efforts to provide additional access to harm-reduction protections , escalating criminal penalties have not produced the treatment gains or decreases in overdose deaths in Colorado that proponents promised
So, let’s look at a place in the state where overdose deaths are actually falling to see what is being done differently there
Larimer County, home of Colorado State University and part of Rocky Mountain National Park, offers the clearest contrast to the rest of the state
Accidental overdose deaths have declined year after year since 2022 , down nearly 42% from 2021
What’s going on in Larimer County? For one, the Larimer County Jail is one of less than half of the Colorado county jails that offers that includes medications for opioid use disorder
The sheriff’s office, in collaboration with several community-based organizations, has also flooded the community with naloxone through the Reversal Project
Furthermore, using opioid abatement funds , the county has expanded youth and family support services, co-responder units and other harm-reduction services
The county has also steadily increased the number of people on buprenorphine
