title: Pennsylvania’s aging prisons weren’t built for today’s extreme weather – leaving women and seniors especially at risk of illness and death
url:
<title>Pennsylvania’s aging prisons weren’t built for today’s extreme weather – leaving women and seniors especially at risk of illness and death</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765016/original/file-20261008-60-aap6mb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3500%2C2333&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People in prison can&#39;t just switch on the air conditioning when it starts to swelter.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/exterior-view-of-chester-county-prison-from-which-convicted-news-photo/1657117984">Mark Makela/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>When outdoor temperatures spike to 103 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius), or drop to -9 F (-23 C), like they did across Pennsylvania last year, people locked up in jails and prisons cannot simply turn on the air conditioning or find a public warming center.</p>

<p>For several years, people in custody, advocates and local media <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2024/07/pennsylvania-prisons-air-conditioning-heatwave">have sounded the alarm</a> about the dangers posed by extreme temperatures in Pennsylvania’s state prisons. </p>

<p>Conditions inside Pennsylvania’s prisons have been described <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2024/07/pennsylvania-prisons-air-conditioning-heatwave">as a sauna</a> during a summer heat wave and bitterly cold in the winter, especially when heating systems have malfunctioned. Amy McBride, a woman in her early 60s incarcerated at MCI Muncy, <a href="https://prisonjournalismproject.org/2025/02/25/extreme-cold-prison/">told the Prison Journalism Project</a>, “I tend to wear two to three layers of pants and four to six layers of shirts (in winter), sometimes with my jacket and coat over them.” </p>

<p>I am an epidemiologist who <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=rhfnW0YAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">studies the health of incarcerated people</a>. My colleagues and I put numbers to these warnings in a recent study. We found that extreme hot and cold temperatures were associated with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78012-y">higher rates of deaths, infirmary admissions and transfers to external medical facilities</a> among imprisoned people in Pennsylvania over the past 20 years. </p>

<p>While these temperature hazards are not unique to Pennsylvania, several factors make this issue a particular concern for the state. Pennsylvania has the nation’s <a href="https://bjs.ojp.gov/library/publications/prisoners-2023-statistical-tables">sixth-largest prison population</a> among U.S. states. Nearly 40,000 people are confined in Pennsylvania prisons. </p>

<p>Furthermore, most of Pennsylvania’s state prison facilities were built in the 1990s or earlier, when weather patterns were not so <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dep/residents/climate-change/impacts">extreme</a>. Some, including the state correctional institutions in <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-cambridge-springs">Cambridge Springs</a>, <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-dallas">Dallas</a>, <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-laurel-highlands">Laurel Highlands</a>, <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-muncy">Muncy</a>, <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-waymart">Waymart</a> and <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-huntingdon">Huntingdon</a>, the oldest continuously running correctional facility in Pennsylvania, have partial or very limited air conditioning. This means they have air conditioning in some buildings or units, such as nursing care areas, and not others.</p>

<p>Previous research also suggests that while hot temperatures <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0281389">pose risks to incarcerated people across the country</a>, those incarcerated in the Northeast have experienced some of the greatest increases in heat-related mortality risk since 2001.</p>

<h2>Prison healthcare systems under strain</h2>

<p>Even under normal weather conditions, prison healthcare systems are highly strained. People in prison are more likely than the general population to have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2017.04.040">chronic medical conditions such as heart disease</a>, and the state’s prison population <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/TR/Transcripts/2024_0522_0002_TSTMNY.pdf">is getting older</a>, which increases its medical needs and expenses. The average age at prison admission has increased from 31 in 2000 to <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/TR/Transcripts/2024_0522_0002_TSTMNY.pdf">38 in 2023</a>.</p>

<p>The average cost for medications alone for adults over 50 in the state’s prison is <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/TR/Transcripts/2024_0522_0002_TSTMNY.pdf">US$3,357 per person per year</a>. That’s <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/TR/Transcripts/2024_0522_0002_TSTMNY.pdf">53% more</a> than costs for younger incarcerated adults. </p>

<p>The state prison system experiences <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/TR/Transcripts/2024_0522_0002_TSTMNY.pdf">chronic staffing shortages</a> of corrections officers, nurses and physicians. Some facilities have experienced vacancy rates of medical staff of nearly 40%. Shortages of corrections officers result in greater restrictions on the movement of incarcerated people, who then have less access to health appointments, group therapy and other programming. This can be especially difficult for <a href="https://prisonjournalismproject.org/2026/03/17/prison-staffing-problems-are-especially-hard-on-lifers/">older incarcerated people and those who have been incarcerated for long periods of time</a>, because they have greater medical needs and are often more isolated from loved ones.</p>

<p>Constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment <a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/USREPORTS-429/USREPORTS-429-97">prohibit deliberate indifference to prisoners’ medical needs</a>. But in addition to staffing shortages and other administrative challenges with healthcare delivery in prisons, incarcerated people also face financial barriers. </p>

<p>In Pennsylvania, they must pay a <a href="https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/cor/documents/about-us/doc-policies/820%20Co-Payment%20for%20Medical%20Services.pdf">$5 copay</a> per visit to receive medical treatment that is determined by the Department of Correction to not be an emergency. This may sound low but is substantial in the context of wages that range from <a href="https://www.prisonsociety.org/updates/doc-raises-wages-for-incarcerated-people">23 cents to 50 cents per hour</a>. </p>

<h2>Incarcerated women may face higher heat risks</h2>

<p>One unexpected finding from our analysis was that women in Pennsylvania state prisons experienced greater increases in rates of infirmary visits and transfers to external medical facilities on and after extremely hot days than men. </p>

<p>This was unexpected because <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000000375">previous studies</a> haven’t consistently shown that women are more vulnerable to heat-related health risks. But these studies were conducted in the general population, not among people in prison.</p>

<p>Incarcerated people experience what medical researchers call “<a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1177/00221465211052568">accelerated aging</a>” because of the stressors they experience during and prior to incarceration. This means their biologic age is ahead of their chronological age. They are more likely to experience menopause, cancer and chronic disease <a href="https://whyy.org/articles/in-prison-women-develop-diseases-earlier-and-often/">at a younger age</a> than would typically be expected. </p>

<p>Hot flashes and night sweats are common symptoms of menopause that can become <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1177/10783458261449636">life threatening</a> during extreme heat events and when cooling, hydration and hormone therapy are limited or unavailable. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Close up shot of healthcare worker's gloved hands handing blister pack of pills to person wearing orange" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C293%2C5616%2C3159&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Extreme heat can turn common symptoms of menopause into health hazards for women in prison.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/close-up-shot-of-healthcare-workers-gloved-hands-royalty-free-image/1397838530">Mindful Media/E+ Collection via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Preparing for a warmer climate</h2>

<p>Our research found that extreme heat and extreme cold increase the demands on an already strained system of prison operations and healthcare delivery. These demands will likely only get worse as extreme temperatures continue to intensify.</p>

<p>We believe climate resilience planning will require improvements in prison conditions, improvements in prison healthcare systems, and policy efforts to reduce the number of people – particularly older adults – who are incarcerated.</p>

title: How to lose a job in five days
excerpt: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing at the White House on October 13, 2026. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images This story appe
body: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing at the White House on October 13, 2026. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is out of a job after only five days.  What happened? Zacharia was fired on Friday after less than a week in her new role, after a rocky start that included a halting performance in the briefing room, a scandal over her legal credentials, and a round of less-than-successful cleanup interviews .  The firing makes her the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in history, outstripping even first-term Trump communications director Anthony Scaramucci, who made it 10 or 11 days (figures vary) before getting the boot.  “Records are made to be broken,” Scaramucci posted on Friday . “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.” (No word yet on whether the “Zacharia” will emerge as a unit of time, as the “Scaramucci” has.)  What’s the context? Zacharia’s remarkably short stint behind the podium unfolded as the White House is engaged in an unprecedented attack on press freedom: The administration is still trying to ban three media outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House, though as of earlier this week, a judge is still blocking the ban from taking effect

The diminished nature of the press secretary job was on full display in Zacharia’s sole briefing on Tuesday , when she took questions from just three outlets: Breitbart, Fox News, and the Daily Mail.  Why does this matter? Zacharia’s no good, very bad week is not likely to leave much of a lasting mark in its own right — other than, perhaps, as pub trivia — but as NBC’s Garrett Haake points out , it’s a very tangible manifestation of a White House that seems to have no idea how to spin itself out of crisis with just weeks until the midterm elections.  Most recently, Trump has landed on flat-out lying about the state of the economy — but like Zacharia’s time as press secretary, it doesn’t seem like it’s going to go all that well

And with that, it’s time to log off… The underlying trend — municipal inaction — may be infuriating, but I loved this story about “tactical urbanism” from my colleague Sara Herschander.  As she writes, vigilante activists have taken to painting their own crosswalks, building benches, and even installing makeshift bike lanes in their neighborhoods — and every time they do, “they remind us that it is not actually that hard — or even that expensive — to do many of the simple things that can make our cities safer and more pleasant places to live.”  You can read Sara’s full piece here , no gift link needed
Enjoy, have a great weekend, and we’ll see you on Monday!

title: West Bank settlers brutally attack a Washington Post journalist
excerpt: Photojournalist Heidi Levine is transferred on a stretcher into an ambulance after she was attacked by Israeli settlers while photographing Palestinian farmers
body: Photojournalist Heidi Levine is transferred on a stretcher into an ambulance after she was attacked by Israeli settlers while photographing Palestinian farmers harvesting their olives on October 16, 2026. | Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
On Friday, Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians living in the West Bank, as well as a Washington Post photographer, who was hospitalized with serious injuries
Photojournalist Heidi Levine was knocked down, beaten, and robbed of her camera equipment by masked settlers in an attack captured on video by other journalists
Those other members of the press rescued her from the attackers while Israel Defense Forces soldiers reportedly stood by
Levine had lacerations and a wound to her hand that split her finger to the bone, according to the Post , which condemned the attack in a statement
Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who helped Levine escape the attack, said that Levine also had cracked ribs, and may have been stabbed
Assaults like this one are becoming more common in the West Bank, where settler violence — which is currently targeting the ongoing olive harvest — has worsened

Last week, another photojournalist for the news wire Agence France-Presse was beaten with rifles by settlers, and Palestinian residents of the West Bank have been shot, beaten, and terrorized while the Israeli settlers targeting them face few consequences
Why settler violence is growing in the West Bank As my colleague Zack Beauchamp recently explained, under international law, the settler movement in the West Bank is clearly illegal
Nevertheless, it’s continued to grow, and it has a friend in the current Israeli government led by Benjamin Netanyahu

It’s also becoming increasingly violent.  Two current Israeli officials, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir, are settlers themselves, and both have used their offices — as ministers of finance and national security, respectively — to  further the settler cause , including by making it easier for settlers to commit unchecked violence against Palestinians.  The United Nations  reported in June that settler attacks had reached “the highest sustained levels ever recorded…with [an average of] six daily attacks that have resulted in casualties, property damage or both,” and in many Palestinians being forced from their homes by settlers

In late September , the International Committee of the Red Cross said that expanding Israeli settlements and violence by settlers was “making everyday life untenable” for Palestinian residents of the West Bank

As Zack has reported , settlements and settler violence are both intentional tactics, serving to force more Palestinians off their land, isolate the ones who stay, and push any potential two-state solution further out of reach.  That kind of violence is likely only to worsen in the weeks to come: Israel will hold elections on October 27, which could well result in Netanyahu’s settler-friendly government losing power
As a result, the Washington Post reported earlier this month , settlers are “racing to lock down gains” before the election with ever more extreme violence
One link for later ➨ Agentified kind of life
My colleague Adam Clark Estes turned the keys to his life over to a passel of AI agents for two weeks to see what would happen

They successfully saved him some times, he writes, largely with mundane tasks — but he left with mixed feelings about the experiment, including the possibility of contributing to a world with more AI slop

body: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network , an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report
Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status

body: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist
